From al-Zajjāj: it is not compounded, and there is no negation of what has been said, that they have idols that benefit them. Jaram is a past-tense verb meaning kasaba (he earned), its subject is an implied pronoun referring to their act, and innahum is its object. Al-Farrā' said: it is a word originally meaning lā budda (there is no escape) and lā maḥālah (there is no doubt), for he transmits from the Arabs lā jurm, meaning with a ḍammah then a sukūn, and the verb, meaning in this manner, and the verb, meaning vowelled, both share in the verbal nouns like al-rushd, al-ra'd, and al-bukhl. Al-jaram is cutting, that is, there is no cutting from this, just as lā budda means there is no cutting. It became common and took this course until it came to have the meaning of an oath, so it is answered with what an oath is answered with. It is said: lā jaram la-ātiyannaka (there is no doubt I will surely come to you), and lā jaram annaka qā'im (there is no doubt that you are standing). Whoever reads it with fatḥah does so in view of the original form of lā jaram, as we say: lā budda an naf'ala kadhā wa-annaka taf'alu, that is, from an and from annaka taf'alu. Whoever reads it with kasrah does so for the meaning of the oath that has arisen in lā jaram. End of quotation.

So his interpretation of it as cutting is considered, in that the root jaram specifically revolves around cutting. The more appropriate interpretation is as doubt, in view of what the root itself revolves around, in whatever order it occurs: jaram, [jamar], rajam, ramaj, majar, and maraj. I have made it so because they said: jaram al-nakhl meant he estimated its yield, and ajmara al-nakhl also meant he estimated its yield; rajama meant when he supposed; al-majar is the intellect, and suspicion entails the kindling of the mind, from which comes jamrat al-nār (ember of fire); al-jarm for the hard ground that is strongly pulled; suspicion also entails the gathering of thought, from which comes al-jamrah for the heart and everything resembling it in gathering; from it comes al-jirm (with kasrah), which is the body, for it is considered in terms of its whole; and the voice, or its loudness, for the throat is gathered in it for cutting; gathering also entails greatness, from which comes ajrama, meaning he became great; al-jamīr, like amīr, is the gathering place of a people; from gathering comes ostentation and intellect, from which clarity arises; from it comes ﴿a flame of fire﴾ [al-Raḥmān 55:15], that is, there is no smoke in it; from it comes ajrama lawnuhu, meaning its color became clear; from gathering comes al-majar (with fatḥah), which is when one fills his belly with water without being satisfied; and earning: jaram li-ahlihi, meaning he earned for his family; from it comes al-dhanb (sin), for it is a specific kind of earning; and it is possible that it is from cutting, because it cuts its doer off from good. Gathering also entails concealment, from which comes ajamarat al-laylah, meaning the crescent was hidden in it. Al-majar is for what is in the bellies of pregnant camels and goats; or this may be considered among what entails the very nature of suspicion, from obscurity. From gathering comes emaciation: ajmara al-khayl means he trained the horses by lean feeding, and shāh mujmarah means a lean sheep. Gathering also entails firmness and completeness, from which comes ḥawl mujram, like mu'ẓam, meaning complete year, from which separation arises. From it comes tajarrama al-layl, meaning the night departed; and ibnā jamīr, like amīr, are the night and the day; or this may be one of the necessary consequences of cutting, as will come. From gathering also comes al-rajm, which is the close friend and companion. Suspicion entails distinguishing between things. From it comes jirām al-nakhl, for its cutting of the dates. Al-jamrah is the pebble, so this entails throwing in general, from which arises throwing the stones (al-jimār), which are stones, from which arises killing the one stoned. This also returns to the very nature of cutting, for it is the cutting of the self from what it was upon. Distinction entails slander and blame. Al-rimāj, like saḥāb, is the knuckles of the spear, due to the separation of some of them from others. Al-ramaj with fatḥah is the bird dropping its dung. Suspicion [entails exaggeration in looking, so exaggeration appears in speech and resolve, from which comes al-mirjām for the camel that extends its neck while traveling; and ajmara means he hastened in travel; and suspicion may entail bewilderment]. From it comes a ḥadīth mujram, like mu'ẓam, meaning one whose reality cannot be grasped. Then sin, corruption, anxiety, and turmoil necessarily follow. From it comes amraja al-'ahd, meaning he did not fulfill the covenant, that is, he made it shaky and unsteady. The root maraja, in this particular arrangement, revolves around turmoil, or al-tarmīj is spoiling lines after they have been written. Suspicion entails confusion, from which comes al-jirm for color, because it is never free of admixture; ajrama al-dam bihi means it stuck to it. Al-ijrām is the herdsman's goods, or it is from earning. Al-jurrām, like rummān, is fish. Al-maraj is the grazing place. It is known from this that all forms of the root revolve around turmoil, and this is clear in everything except the intellect. As for the intellect, it is considered as turmoil of opinion, because the intelligent person, whenever he examines carefully, has opened to him what was closed, so he turns toward it. When this is clear, it becomes evident that the meaning of lā jaram is: there is no suspicion and no turmoil regarding the fact that they [annahum]. The negation of suspicion in such a context is the negation of everything opposed to it, except the knowledge that is in the sense of certainty, just as when one says: there is no doubt in such and such and no uncertainty. It is thus clarified that their interpretation of it as "truly" is an interpretation of meaning for the two words combined. For when suspicion is negated in such a context, certainty and conviction are established. To this returns Sībawayh's interpretation as "no right," for he means, God knows best, that it is not a connective particle (ṣilah), and its original function is negation. It negates the opposite of what it enters upon. So it is as if it were said: it is true and established that they are such and such, and everything opposed to it is negated. This is the way in which it is an emphatic connective. Similar to this is what has been said about innamā, as in: innamā Zayd qā'im, meaning: Zayd is standing, and nothing else is the case. Thus it has become clear that the negating particle, in the same way, is emphatic. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 23:

When He had threatened the disbelievers and informed of their end because of their conduct, it was fitting to ask about the condition of the believers, so He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, i.e., they brought this reality into existence, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾. Since what had preceded in describing the disbelievers, after mere evil deeds, was turning away from their Lord and aversion to the One who does good to them, out of coarseness and harshness, He described the believers by turning toward Him and being at rest with Him, and so He said: ﴿and humble themselves﴾, i.e., they were submissive, turning [to Him], cutting off [all else], ﴿to their Lord﴾, i.e., the One who does good to them, so they gave thanks to Him, and He granted them success in the capacity of hearing and sight.

When He mentioned their description, He mentioned their reward for it by His saying: ﴿Those﴾, i.e., the exalted in rank, ﴿are the companions of Paradise﴾. Since they were specifically [destined] for it from the beginning, or for eternity from the outset of the matter, He repeated the pronoun and said: ﴿They therein﴾, i.e., specifically and not in anything else, ﴿abide forever﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 24:

When he had fully described the two parties and their recompense, he set forth a parable for both by saying: ﴿The likeness of the two parties﴾, that is, the disbelievers and the believers. This is of the type of the arranged "folding and unfolding" (al-laff wa'l-nashr al-murattab), for the disbeliever was mentioned earlier first as ﴿like the blind﴾, that is, one completely blind in his sight and his insight, and ﴿the deaf﴾ in his hearing likewise. This applies to the disbelievers. Then ﴿the seeing﴾ with his eye and his heart, and ﴿the hearing﴾ in the fullest of their conditions. This applies to the believers. And within the individual terms of the parable there is also antithesis (tibaq). ﴿Are the two equal﴾, that is, the two parties, ﴿in likeness﴾, that is: in terms of the parable? Since the answer is a certainty for anyone with even slight reflection, namely that they are not equal as a likeness, therefore they are not equal as the thing likened, the rebuke is well-founded when it is stated in His saying: ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾, that is: let there arise in you at least some measure of remembrance through what the idgham (assimilation) indicates, so that you know the truth of what they have been described with, by what you see of their conditions. This is what was earlier presented concerning the disbelievers in His saying: ﴿They were not able to hear﴾ [Hud: 20], and so on.

Al-ikhbat (humility) is continuous submissiveness that is steady in its composure; its root is "istiwa'" (evenness) from al-khabt, which is the wide, level land. Perhaps he connected it with "ila" in the place of the lam as an indication of sincerity; that is: humility that reaches its Lord without being veiled from Him. And the mathal (proverb or parable) is a well-known saying in which the state of the second is likened to the state of the first, and proverbs are not altered from their form.

When this had been completed in the clearest manner, and concluded with an exhortation to remembrance, and the mention of the Book of Moses had been placed first, which prompted the expectation of mention of his story and the story of the other messengers, it was connected (accompanied by the particle of expectation, *qad*) to the governing element that I estimated in His saying ﴿Do not worship except Allah﴾ [Hud: 2], or to His saying ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Hud: 12]. The latter is better and closer. His saying ﴿And We certainly sent﴾ means, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿Noah to his people﴾, that is, those who were upon his tongue. What follows of the narratives serves to confirm the content of this example, to establish it, to console, support, and comfort this noble Prophet, so that his chest would not be constricted by anything of what he was commanded to convey, out of eagerness for the faith of anyone, even if that person were the closest of creatures to him and the dearest to him. This was indicated earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let there be no constriction in your chest from it﴾ [al-A'raf: 2], and His saying: ﴿And your chest is constricted by it﴾ [Hud: 12]. It will also come in His saying: ﴿And We relate to you from the news of the messengers that which We strengthen your heart with﴾ [Hud: 120]. Thus it became clear that these narratives were brought for this meaning, and that their context in al-A'raf and elsewhere was for something other than this, as was previously explained. The inclusion of this purpose is the demonstration of the destruction of those who were stronger than the Arabs in power, greater in numbers, more capable in affairs, stronger in obstinacy, greater in corruption, and sharper in might, and of the calamities and dreadful catastrophes that befell their dwellings, as a warning against the likes of their state through committing their deeds. Thus there is a distinction between what is brought for a thing and what necessarily follows from a thing. For this intended purpose here, the story of Noah was lengthened in this surah more than it was lengthened in any other. It was introduced with His saying ﴿Indeed I﴾, that is, saying, according to the reading of the majority (al-Jumhur, the majority of reciters) with the kasra. The estimate according to Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i is: connected with the fact that I am ﴿to you﴾, that is, specifically, ﴿a clear warner﴾, that is, a warner of eloquent warning, I make clear what I was sent with in the utmost clarity. He mentioned in it that his disputation with them was prolonged, and that when the command of Allah became clear to him, he sought refuge from asking about it and everything resembling it. His story was interspersed with His saying: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [Hud: 35], addressed to this noble Prophet, and it was concluded with His saying: ﴿So be patient, for indeed the final outcome is for the righteous﴾ [Hud: 49]. The story of Abraham, peace be upon him, was mentioned because of what it contained: that he was given the good news of a son by a means not customary to occur, so he did not hesitate concerning it; and that he argued with the messengers concerning the people of his nephew Lot; and that when the decree of the matter was certain and the judgment was final, he submitted to his Lord, while being forbearing, plaintive, and penitent, along with other matters that the context of the narratives indicates. So it is as if it was said: You are only a warner, We sent you so that you would convey what you were sent with of warning, even if it was difficult for them. By Our might, We certainly sent before you messengers as warners, and they called to what you were commanded to call to, and warned them of what is grievous to them of Our punishment, in compliance with Our command, and they did not abandon any of it out of fear of aversion, nor hope for acceptance. Their nations said to them what your nation said to you, as His exalted saying about Noah indicates: ﴿And I do not say to you, "With me are the treasuries of Allah"﴾ [Hud: 31], and so on. Among those who opposed them of their nations were those closest to them in lineage and those whose affair was dearest to them, from a son, a wife, and others. Moreover, their stories are evidence for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, the day it comes to them, it will not be averted from them﴾ [Hud: 8], and a rebuke to them against saying the likes of their statement: ﴿What is holding it back?﴾ [Hud: 8], and a confirmation of His saying: ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses, as a leader and a mercy﴾ [Hud: 17], and other matters that preceded. Thus it has been known from this aspect, in the repetition of these narratives, that in each surah it is for a purpose that differs from the purpose in others. Although benefit may be drawn from this, there are other benefits as well: among them is the manifestation of power in demonstrating inimitability by turning the meaning through various forms, because of the high rank of eloquence in it. For perhaps a contentious person might say when challenged: "These narratives have exhausted the eloquent wording in the most complete and wondrous style, so no words remain for us with which to express these meanings to the point that we could produce the like of this narrative." So He brought it a second time, to demonstrate their incapacity and to sever their argument. It may be repeated a third and fourth time for emphasis, for establishing the lesson through various modes of exposition, and to make the Prophet (ﷺ) patient over the harm of his people, step by step. If it is said: Why do they come at times in the utmost detail, and at other times in the utmost brevity, and at other times in a middle form? It is said: This is from the highest degrees of eloquence and the most exalted ranks of fluency and skill. If it is said: We see that a narrative is expanded to the utmost detail in some surahs, and then condensed to the utmost brevity in others, and in them there is what is not in the expanded version, as in al-'Ankabut, where He specified the length of his stay, that it was a thousand years less fifty years. Then why did it not comprehend all the meanings in the expanded place, as is most fitting for the position of expansion, especially for one from whom nothing is hidden and who does not forget? And if omission occurs, it is in the condensed version. It is said: Our shaykh, the hafiz of the age, Abu al-Fadl ibn Hajar, said: Imam Abu Hatim ibn Hibban al-Busti mentioned in his book "al-Taqasim wa al-Anwa'" (The Divisions and Types): "He only did not arrange it so that it could be memorized. For if he had arranged it in an easy order, whoever has it would rely on the ease of retrieving from it and would not memorize it. When the path of retrieval is difficult, it is more conducive to memorizing it, so that one would be mindful of all of it." He mentioned that he did this in emulation of the Noble Book, for it sometimes brings narratives not in order. Our shaykh said: From here it becomes clear that among the secrets of specifying some condensed narratives with what is not in the expanded ones is the exhortation to memorize all of them. End of quote. These are benefits that should not be neglected, rather they are to be used wherever possible. The foundation regarding the correspondence (munasabah) is the first aspect, which is that they occur in each surah for a correspondence specific to that surah. Then, in expansion and otherwise, one considers the meanings that correspond to the purpose for which the narrative was brought. And Allah is the Granter of success.

The lam in "laqad" is for oath. Imam Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn 'Isa al-Rummani said: Because it enters upon the verb and upon the particle that is specific to the verb, whose meaning is valid with it. The lam of inception (lam al-ibtida') is specific to the noun. The meaning of "qad" is anticipation of the report, for proximity to the present state, as one says: "Qad rakiba al-amir" (The commander has indeed mounted), to a people who anticipate his mounting. On this view, "Wa-laqad arsalna" proceeds. Al-Ibanah (clarification) is the manifestation of meaning to the self by means that can be grasped; its origin is severance. So clarification is the severing of a meaning from others so that it appears in itself. End of quote.

The purpose of the message is His (glorified is He) statement: ﴿that﴾, meaning: a warner, so that ﴿you worship not﴾, meaning: anything at all, ﴿except Allah﴾, meaning: the Supreme King. [The meaning of warning] is His statement: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you﴾, and the magnitude of the punishment he warns of in His statement: ﴿the punishment of a painful day﴾. If the day is painful, what must be thought of the punishment within it! This is a figurative attribution (isnad majazi, a transfer of a verbal attribute from its true subject to something associated with it), like "its day is fasting." He did not mention good news (p. 269), as had been mentioned earlier from the Prophet ﷺ in His statement: ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ [Hud: 2], as a guide to what the story was brought to establish, namely the affirmation of the meaning of ﴿You are but a warner﴾ [Hud: 12]. For this reason he explicitly mentioned the pain, unlike in al-A'raf, and likewise what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded at the beginning of this surah regarding ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾; the two are close in meaning. Then He (glorified is He) related the answer of his people in a manner that is most consoling and fitting to the context, with His statement: ﴿So said﴾, meaning: as a consequence of this great counsel, they said. Since this was after some of them had followed him, He said: ﴿the eminent ones﴾, and He showed that disputing with error, after showing that they were the nobles, is further consolation, with His statement: ﴿who disbelieved﴾, and He showed that they were powerful relatives with His statement: ﴿from among his people﴾, meaning: those who are in the utmost strength to attempt what they intend. ﴿We see you not﴾, meaning: anything of things, ﴿except a human being﴾, meaning: a son of Adam, ﴿like us﴾, meaning: in the general sense of humanity. You are not an angel, so as to be fit for what you are not fit for of the message. This is the statement of the al-Barahimah (Brahmins), and it is the denial of the prophethood of humans in absolute terms, and it is the statement of one who envies the bounty of God and is blind to the clear wisdom of it, so he denies that the Prophet can be a human and makes God a stone.

Since greatness among them was confined to the greatness of followers, they said: ﴿and we do not see you﴾. And since they negated seeing him, the listener was eager for what they meant by it, so they clarified that their intended meaning was the seeing of those who followed him, and so they said: ﴿who follow you﴾, meaning (p. 270) who have burdened themselves with following you, ﴿except those who are﴾, meaning: specifically, ﴿our lowest ones﴾, meaning: like the weaver and the like, and there is none among us of baseness other than them. It is the plural of arhal (lowest), like akhlub is the plural of radhl, as kalb (dog) [has plural akhlub]; al-radhl means the base and mean. This entails that no one of rank has followed you. They said: "who follow you" governs His statement: ﴿at first sight﴾, and it is an adverb of time, meaning: they followed you immediately without reflection. Their following does not indicate soundness of what they followed, for two reasons: their baseness in themselves, and that they did not reflect upon it. However, it is weakened by the mention of the following in the form of ifti'al, which indicates effort and pulling, so the better attribution is to attribute it, as they also said, to the lowest ones. That is, they are such that the observer, at the first glance of his eyes upon them, does not pause to consider that they are base, degraded. It is also possible that the meaning is "at first sight of yours," meaning that you think they followed you, and they did not follow you.

Since they only regarded eminence as coming from worldly expansion, they said: ﴿and we see for you﴾, meaning: for you and for those who follow you, ﴿over us﴾, and they went to excess in negation with their statement: ﴿any superiority﴾, meaning: of nobility or wealth. This, together with what preceded of their statements, is the statement of one who knows the truth by men and does not know men by the truth, because he infers that a thing is true from the greatness of its followers in this world, and that it is false from their insignificance in it. The totality of their statements indicates that they mean: if prophethood could be in a human, it would be in one of those whom they acknowledged as high on earth. The governing of "who follow you" over "at first sight" prevents the continuation of following upon faith, so the accusation of lack of reflection is removed. ﴿Rather, we think you are liars﴾, meaning: this description is constantly permanent for you, because you do not possess what we made the sign of following, of what necessitates greatness in hearts and submission of souls through precedence in this world by wealth and station. Their disease was thus the rejection of truth (batar al-haqq) and contempt for people (ghamt al-nas), which is their looking down upon them. This has spread to most of the people of Islam, so they honor none except by that, and this is the greatest ignorance, because the messengers came to renounce the world. And look at their contentment with themselves in turning away from the clear proof to following conjecture; how vile it is! And this is more hideous than what is related here of the Quraysh's statement: ﴿Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?﴾ [Hud: 12], and more abominable.

And "bashar" (human) means a human being, because of the visibility of his skin (bashara), that is, the outer surface of his hide, since what predominates on other animals is their covering with wool, hair, fur or feathers. And "mithl" means that which fills the place of another in perception, in the sense that if it appeared to observation it would fill its place. And "radhl" means the contemptible, with what is upon him of attributes of deficiency, and its plural. And "fadl" means excess of good, and "ifdal" means multiplying good which necessitates gratitude.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 28:

When the conclusion of their reply was at its harshest, he began his answer by refuting them, making their errors clear while overlooking their outrageous statements, out of compassion for them and love for their salvation. So God, the Exalted, said, relating his words: ﴿He said, "O my people!"﴾ He kept repeating this address every little while, reminding them that he was one of them, so that ties of kinship would move them and family bonds would turn them, away from envy or accusation, toward accepting the words he was conveying to them. He used the particle of distance, despite their nearness, to indicate their remoteness in matters that call for the utmost closeness. ﴿Tell me﴾, that is: inform me, ﴿if I am﴾ on the basis of supposition from your side and assumption, ﴿upon a clear proof﴾, that is: a shining demonstration. He added to encourage acceptance of it with his words ﴿from my Lord﴾, that is, the One who brought me into being and was good to me with prophethood and other things, bearing witness to the truth of my claim with a testimony [that] no doubt can reach, in the eyes of the fair-minded, let alone mere conjecture! ﴿And has given me﴾ grace from Him toward me, not because of any merit in me that would make me superior to you, but ﴿mercy﴾, that is: honor through messengership after prophethood. He magnified it with his words ﴿from Himself﴾, indicating that it carries great grace, with clearly manifest radiance.

Since the clear proof was a form of mercy, he used the singular pronoun and said: ﴿but it has been obscured﴾, that is: as a consequence of my being singled out with it, its darkness has fallen, ﴿upon you﴾, that is: you have become blind to it because of the weakness of your minds, and none of its light reached you. This is because when the guide is blind, its harm returns upon the follower in bewilderment and error. This is the meaning of the reading of Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim, with the passive form and doubled consonant: ﴿shall we compel you to it﴾. His words ﴿while you are averse to it﴾, together with his naming it a clear proof, indicate that it did not become general nor was it hidden from them, because of the strength of its light and the intensity of its manifestation. Rather, they are obstinate in denying his grace and the grace of those who followed him. The expression of this by a nominal sentence (p. 273) and an active participle indicates that their actions stem from a dislike of it that is firm and established. It seems he was not commanded to fight, as our Prophet (ﷺ) was at the beginning of the matter. The verse looks to God's saying: ﴿Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ [Yunus: 99]. It is also possible that this is a metaphor for their being obstinate, quite apart from fighting and other things, for the prophets (peace be upon them) are commanded to dispute with the obstinate until they establish the proof against them, and this only yields compulsion outwardly while denial and dislike remain inwardly; and to call to the path of God with wisdom for the perfected, and with exhortation and admonition for the hypocrites who are not obstinate and think well of the one calling them. The meaning, then, is that the clear proof did not benefit you because of the harshness and crookedness of your natures, so nothing remains but exhortation, which benefits only with good opinion. As for when there is aversion, counsel does not benefit you, and there is no use in debate except compulsion, which, with aversion, is of no benefit to you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 29:

Since the negation of that applies generally to worldly advantage, and since being characterized by scarcity of what is in one's hand is only harmful when its possessor asks others for it, [al-Biqa'i] negated this concomitant defect from him. [Noo] said, answering their negation of advantage from him and from his followers, on the grounds that he might seek from them a worldly reward for that: ﴿And O my people﴾, appealing to their sympathy, ﴿I do not ask you﴾, i.e., at any time, ﴿for it﴾, i.e., for the warning, as one who warns you takes from you when he wants to warn you about a matter that intends for you some of what you dislike in the affairs of your worldly life, so that the outcome of that would be that you accuse me, ﴿wealth, if not﴾, i.e., nothing, ﴿my reward is except from God﴾, i.e., the One who possesses majesty and honor, so all the treasuries are in His hand. By this he drew attention to the fact that he has no aim from any worldly goods that would repel the one he invites, so his truthfulness became necessary to accept. In this there is an instruction for the answer to the statement of Quraysh, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him?" as will come more clearly after the story of Joseph, peace be upon him, in His saying: ﴿And you do not ask them for any reward for it﴾ [Yusuf: 104], because these stories are like one thing, consecutive in clarifying the truth of this Qur'an and the consolation in following the Messengers in patience in conveying the whole message, along with what that necessitates of noble lessons and wondrous wisdom. So when the aim from them was united along with their succession, their scattered parts became united.

Since the expression of the lowliness of the followers was among what repels the people of the world from that follower, [Noo] made clear to them that his condition is not their condition, and that he is gentle toward whoever believes in him, kind to him, and merciful to him, even if he is behind in worldly matters and deprived of them, out of fear of God, whom they followed in this. So he said: ﴿And I am not﴾, and he went to the extreme in negation with his saying: ﴿one who drives away those who believed﴾, i.e., those who affirmed with their tongues the faith. Then he gave the reason for that with his saying, emphasizing against their denial: ﴿that they are going to meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46], i.e., the One who does good to them after bringing them into being and arranging them for their guidance, so if I were to drive them away, they would complain about me to Him. So I see no basis for you in pointing to driving them away, nor in anything of what you have answered me with. ﴿But I see you﴾, i.e., I know you with a knowledge that is like sight, ﴿as a people who are ignorant﴾ [i.e.] you act the deeds of the people of ignorance, so you deny the truthful, you reproach the believers with what does not concern them, you forget the meeting with God, and you place things in other than their proper places. In his expression "you are ignorant" (tajhalun) rather than "ignorant" (jahilin), there is an indication that ignorance is renewed for them and is not their habit, appealing to them toward forbearance.

Then he turned to explicit pleading, in a context warning against the seizures of God, and said: ﴿And O my people﴾, meaning, those who are the most dear of people to me, ﴿who will help me against God﴾, meaning, the One who possesses all greatness, ﴿if I drive them away﴾, even though they have not complained about me to Him, since He is aware of what is subtle and what is great. When the answer to their contempt was complete, he based on it a denunciation for their not remembering what he had told them, through what they find within themselves, and so he said: ﴿Will you not remember?﴾, meaning: even with the slightest remembrance, which the idgham (assimilation of the letters) points to, so that you would know that whoever drives away a friend of yours, you have opposed him and intended him harm. Then you would return from the ignorance that has befallen you to your customary forbearance, which prompts reflection that leads to the truth. The ṭard (driving away) is the removal of a thing in a manner of humiliation. The qawm (people) are the group who take up a matter; it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. The tadhkīr (reminding) is the seeking of a meaning that was already present to the soul, while the tafakkur (reflection) is the seeking of it even if it was not present.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 31:

Since their denial of superiority encompassed both wealth and knowledge of the unseen, He confirmed them in that, drawing their attention to their error in it, namely that he had never said among them anything that could be a cause for it. So He said, linking it to His words, "I do not ask you for any wealth for it" (Hud 11:29): ﴿And I do not tell you﴾, that is, at any time whatsoever, ﴿that with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾, that is, of the Greatest King, so that I might bestow favour upon you with them.

Since it is permissible for Allah to empower whomever He wills with treasures of provisions and the like, it is valid for him to be described metaphorically as possessing that dominion, but it is not permissible for Him to empower him with knowledge of the unseen, which is what is hidden from all of creation, because it is exclusively His, glorified is He. He said, linking it to "I say" and not to what is said: ﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾, neither literally nor metaphorically, so that I would know the time of what you are threatened with, or what is in the hearts of the believers of the evil that may be suspected of them. He informed them that there is no impediment to sending a human being by His words: ﴿Nor do I say that I am an angel﴾, so that my strength would be superior to your strength, or my creation greater in worth than your creation, and the like of that from the outward superiority which you have made to be the superiority. So the verse is not evidence for the superiority of the angels. The secret of dropping "for you" has been mentioned in al-An'am.

Since their disparaging remark denying him angelhood was a form of belittlement, He followed it with an affirmation of accepting whoever believes, whoever he may be, even if they despise him, by His words: ﴿Nor do I say to those whom your eyes look down upon﴾, that is, concerning those whom ﴿your eyes look down upon﴾, meaning you hold in contempt and fall short of regarding them as worthy of favour when you look at them and find fault with them, ﴿Allah will never give them any good﴾, that is, the One who possesses all perfection. Since it was as if it were said, "What is the matter with you that you do not say that?", He answered with what implies the following: because I know their inner selves and do not judge except by the outward: ﴿Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything, ﴿knows best﴾, that is, even better than they do, ﴿what is in their souls﴾. It is known that He does not wrong anyone, so whoever has good in his soul, He will reward him for it. It is possible that this refers to ﴿the apparent view﴾ (Hud 11:27) in relation to him, peace and blessings be upon him, as has been mentioned: [then he gave the reason for his refraining from that by saying, emphasising their denial of his wronging them on that assumption]: ﴿Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers﴾, that is, if I said that to them, I would be among the transgressors in placing a thing other than its proper place. And "khaza'in" (treasuries) are the fine containers of goods, and the treasuries of Allah are His capabilities, since from them He brings into existence whatever He wills; in describing them thus there is eloquence. And "al-ghayb" (the unseen) is the disappearance of a thing from perception; from it comes "al-shahid" (the witnessed), the opposite of "al-gha'ib" (the absent). When it is said "'ilm ghayb" (knowledge of the unseen), its meaning is knowledge without instruction. And "al-izdira'" is contempt, and it is an iftial form from "al-zira'ya", as in "zaraytu 'alayhi" when you find fault with him, and "azraytu 'alayhi" when you fall short with him. And "al-malak" (angel) is originally "ma'lak", from "al-alukah", which is a message.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 32–33:

When he had fully refuted what they had established in their own view by their response, with the utmost fairness, gentleness and entreaty, he resumed relating their words, saying: ﴿They said﴾ [i.e., the speech of one who found in his rejection no doubt to put forward and no means of evasion]: ﴿O Noah, you have disputed with us﴾, i.e., you intended to twist us and turn us away from our opinions by argument, and we intended to turn you away from your opinion by the same means. ﴿And you have multiplied our disputation﴾, i.e., as a consequence of that [and of our impatience], you have greatly multiplied ﴿our disputation﴾, i.e., our speech in the form of disputation. ﴿So bring us﴾, i.e., as a consequence of that [and] our impatience, that we say to you: your claim has not been established for us. Bring us ﴿that with which you threaten us﴾ of punishment ﴿if you are﴾, i.e., in a state that is innate to you, ﴿of the truthful﴾, i.e., of those deeply rooted in truthfulness in that it will come to us. Thus they openly displayed the obstinacy that removes one from fairness and from being characterized by rectitude, and they called him by his name and would not allow themselves to say to him, "O son of our paternal uncle," even once, just as he had repeatedly said to them, "O my people." The meaning was: we are not receptive to anything that you say, even if you multiply it and prolong it, without any proof from them but rather out of obstinacy and arrogance. So do not weary yourself, but shorten the matter of what you threaten us with. They called it a promise, mockingly, meaning that what you have made a threat is, in our view, a good promise, which we take as a matter of our wishing for its occurrence. The meaning is that you are not capable of that, nor are you truthful in it; so if it is true, then bring it.

It is as if it were said: what did he say to them? So it was said: ﴿He said﴾, following the pattern of his saying: ﴿I do not say to you that I have the treasures of God, nor do I know the unseen﴾ [Hud: 31], ﴿Only God will bring it to you﴾, i.e., He who has comprehensive encompassment of everything, so he disavowed power and strength and referred that to the One to whom it belongs. By his saying ﴿if He wills﴾ he indicated that He is free to bring it about, even though his earlier saying had mentioned it, as guidance that He, glorified is He, is under no obligation to anything and nothing about Him is objectionable, and He is not to be questioned about what He does [although only what He has informed of will occur]. Then he made clear to them their weakness and their error in exposing themselves to destruction, saying: ﴿and you cannot escape﴾, i.e., at any time, from anything that He, glorified is He, wills to do to you. Al-Ikthar (multiplication) is increase beyond the measure of sufficiency. Al-mujadalah (disputation) is confronting with that which turns the opponent from his position by proof or by dubious argument; it is from al-jadal, which is intense twisting. Its aim is the return from a position, whereas the aim of hijaj (argumentation) is the manifestation of proof. It may be blameworthy, like mira' (contentious wrangling), when it is used to cast doubt upon the truth after it has become manifest; and where disputation is restricted by ﴿in the best manner﴾ [al-Isra: 53], its purpose is the manifestation of the truth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 34:

When he had made clear that they are only in His grip, glory be to Him, he increased in explaining His greatness, and that His will dissolves every will before it, in a context indicating that by this he is advising them and that his advice is specific to them. So he said, in answer to what they had imagined, that his arguing with them was speech without benefit: ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you﴾. He mentioned his own will regarding what he wished to mention of the will of God, so he said: ﴿if I desire﴾ [i.e., I combine to the act of advising the will] ﴿to advise you﴾ by informing of the place of error so that it may be avoided, and of guidance so that it may be followed. Its answer (jaza') is omitted, its estimate being: my counsel will not benefit you ﴿if God﴾, i.e., He to whom all command belongs, ﴿desires to lead you astray﴾, i.e., to misguide you and to make you incline away from what is right [for His will, glory be to Him, overcomes my will and my act together]. Nothing will benefit you, as an indication that you are not able to repel the punishment by strength so that you would be victorious, nor by obedience so that you would be beloved and brought near, if God desires to destroy you by misguidance, even if I desire your salvation. He did not say "and my counsel will not benefit you if I advise you," indicating that I do not possess except my own will to advise you. So when I desire it, the furthest that results from my act is that the advice occurs and is sincere toward you. As for benefit from it, nothing of that is up to me; rather it follows the will of God. If He wills your misguidance, it occurs without doubt, and what might result from the advice, namely the advised person acting upon it, which would bring benefit and ward off harm, does not take place. Then he encouraged them to His goodness and warned them of His vengeance, giving the reason for the absence of what He does not will: ﴿He is your Lord﴾, i.e., the one who brought you into existence and manages your affairs, so He alone disposes as He wills.

Since the estimate was: from Him is your origin, he followed it with His words: ﴿and to Him﴾, i.e., not to other than Him, ﴿you will be returned﴾, i.e., with the easiest and least of matters, by death and then resurrection, and He will recompense you for your deeds, as is the custom of kings with their agents.

The content of this verse is close to that of His saying: ﴿You are only a warner, and Allah is Trustee over all things﴾ [Hud: 12]. The warner (nadhir) is one who gives sincere counsel to the one he warns, and the trustee (wakil) is the one to whom matters are entrusted and to whom one returns concerning the thing committed to him. What precedes this verse is an allusion to attributing fabrication (iftira') to Nuh, peace be upon him. Allah followed it with what He mentioned of that attribution, and as an indication that all these stories serve as consolation regarding the duty of warning and as comfort. It is as if it were said: "Do they say to you such words? They said them to Nuh as you see." Then He mentioned the warning that Nuh gave them, with which they did not comply in abandoning anything of what We commanded him, whether it pleased them or angered them. So you have an example in him, and he is sufficient as a model for you, in that you should regard their speech as nothing and devote yourself to what We sent you with, namely giving sincere counsel through warning. ﴿Or do they say﴾ about the Qur'an ﴿"He has invented it"﴾, persisting in what they fabricated. Then the proof crushed it and the argument refuted it. It is as if it were said: "Yes, they do say that." So it was said: "Do not be concerned about it, for it is a saying they intend only as mere obstinacy, while they know its falsity after the proofs that were established against them, by which they attained the certainty of sight (ʿayn al-yaqin). Do not let their saying trouble you, for they make it a means to get you to abandon some of what is revealed to you. So do not do that. Rather, ﴿say﴾ in reply to their saying, ﴿"If I have invented it"﴾, that is, I have cut off its falsehood, ﴿then upon me is my crime﴾, that is, its consequence and its punishment, specifically for me, not for you. And if a crime should overcome me, it would become known to people of intellect and would be manifest in a way by which I would be disgraced. Yet you know best that I am far from that, more distant than the gathering of two opposites or the lifting of two contradictions, because of what you know of me: the purity of my dispositions, the loftiness of my aspirations, the goodness of my reputation, the nobility of my rank, and the honor of my affairs. This would be so even if I were able to do it, so how much more so when I and you are equally incapable of it. ﴿And I am innocent﴾, that is, in the utmost innocence, ﴿of what you commit﴾, that is, of what you bring about as crime. There is no harmful consequence of your crime upon me, after I have made it clear to you and uncovered for you the veil of doubts. Its harm is only upon you. So act with remembrance of this meaning. The way their answer is framed in this manner is more grievous to them than establishing another argument, because they understand from it that it is a binding of them to disgrace, since they are silenced before anyone who has understanding. It is possible that the sense is: "Has your people, O Muhammad, come to their senses and known the ugliness of such a condition, and that it is the condition of the obstinate, so that they returned out of nobility from engaging in such things, and out of shame?" ﴿Or do they say "He has invented it"﴾, that is, they lied about it deliberately, persisting in obstinacy and continuing in alienation, just as the people of Nuh persisted, so that there befalls them what befell them. That is, have they returned to this extent from the story of the people of Nuh, or do they persist in what they attributed to you at the beginning of the surah of fabricating it? Then they would need the story to be completed with what befell them of punishment, so that they might fear a like calamity. The fabrication of falsehood (iftira') is its being fashioned from the self, so it is more specific than falsehood in general, because it may be imitation of another.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 36–37:

When he had finished with this sentence, which is the purpose of this entire context even though it is parenthetical within this narrative, he returned to completing the story as an explanation, because Noah (peace be upon him) was openly declaring to his people everything he had been commanded, even though this was extremely burdensome for them, to the point that there was never any hope on their part that he would leave out any part of it. It also served as a warning to everyone who heard their story, lest what befell them befall him. He said: ﴿And it was revealed﴾, i.e., by the One besides whom there is no revealer, who is the King of kings, ﴿to Noah﴾ after those calamities, ﴿that he will not believe﴾ in what I have brought, ﴿from your people, except those who﴾. Since the one who grants a person what he asks for usually gives some signs before granting it, so that the petitioner expects the granting, He said: ﴿Already believed, so do not﴾, i.e., because of your knowledge that their wretchedness has been fulfilled, We say to you: [do not] ﴿be distressed﴾, i.e., let no misery befall you, meaning severe hardship whose burden would weigh heavily on you through your great contemplation of its consequences, ﴿over what they used to﴾, i.e., over what they were disposed to, ﴿do﴾. For We will take your right from them soon. It seems He had informed him that if they did not respond, He would drown them and save him and those with him in an ark that would carry them upon the surface of the water. So He said: ﴿And construct the ark﴾ while you are ﴿under Our eyes﴾, We protecting you from going astray in its making. The word is in the plural for emphasis on protection and care, by way of figurative expression. ﴿And Our revelation﴾, for We inspire you with the best way of making it, and you know what greatness We have, which overcomes everything and which nothing can exceed; so do not worry that you do not know its craft. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, it is reported that Allah revealed to him to make it like the breast (ju'ju') of a bird, i.e., its chest. He also indicated his compassion for his people and his love for their salvation, as was the condition of this noble prophet with his community. So He said: ﴿And do not address Me﴾, i.e., with any kind of address, even a little, ﴿concerning those who wronged﴾, i.e., who brought about wrongdoing and persisted in it, seeking that I save them. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition: that the judgment concerning them has been settled. So He said: ﴿Indeed, they are to be drowned﴾; the matter has been finalized accordingly.

Ibtiʾas (ibtiʾās, distress accompanied by submission) is sorrow with meekness, because the root of bu's (bu's, misery) is poverty and humiliation. Wahy (waḥy, revelation) is the casting of a meaning into the soul in concealment; it may be understanding without speech through a gesture or the like, and it may be by a hidden speech. Al-Fulk (al-fulk, the ship) is a vessel; it may be feminine or masculine, and its singular and plural are the same, and its root is circling, from falakah (a rounded object).

So He said: ﴿And do not address Me﴾, i.e., with any kind of address, even a little, ﴿concerning those who wronged﴾, i.e., who brought about wrongdoing and persisted in it, seeking that I save them. Then He gave the reason for the prohibition: that the judgment concerning them has been settled. So He said: ﴿Indeed, they are to be drowned﴾; the matter has been finalized accordingly.

Ibtiʾas (ibtiʾās, distress accompanied by submission) is sorrow with meekness, because the root of bu's (bu's, misery) is poverty and humiliation. Wahy (waḥy, revelation) is the casting of a meaning into the soul in concealment; it may be understanding without speech through a gesture or the like, and it may be by a hidden speech. Al-Fulk (al-fulk, the ship) is a vessel; it may be feminine or masculine, and its singular and plural are the same, and its root is circling, from falakah (a rounded object).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 38–40:

When God commanded him and forbade him, He informed that he complied with that, by His saying, linking it to what is understood as: so he despaired of the faith of any of them, so he left off calling them and began to console himself: ﴿And he was making﴾, that is, making the work of one who is extremely skilled, who has a great mastery in that craft, ﴿the ship﴾. So his action is described as occurring while he knew that God, glory be to Him, had decided the matter, namely that he was doing what He had commanded him, (p-284) and that He did not address Him concerning them, nor did he grieve over them. He indicated that they had increased in transgression by His saying: ﴿And whenever﴾, that is, while the situation was that whenever ﴿there passed by him a group﴾, that is, notables, ﴿of his people﴾. The "whenever" (kullama) is answered by His saying: ﴿they ridiculed him﴾, that is, their nobility did not prevent them from this. That is because they saw him toiling at what they had never seen the like of before, so that it would sail upon the water while he was on dry land, and it was of a great and fearsome form. Al-Hasan reported that its length was one thousand two hundred cubits and its width six hundred. They said: "O Nuh! What are you making?" He said: "I am building a house upon the water." It is also permissible that ﴿they ridiculed﴾ be a description of "a group" (mala'), and the answer to "whenever" is ﴿he said﴾. When God had made him despair of their good, he abandoned his softness toward them and his entreating them, and so it became known that this was only for Him, glory be to Him. So He said, relating about him, as a fresh statement: ﴿He said: "If you ridicule us,"﴾. Since they were thinking that he was absorbed in his work, [in their view] he was a target of disgrace and mockery. He, ﷺ, knew that their work was a cause of their humiliation through the uprooting punishment. So the meaning is: "If you ridicule us, that is, me and those who assist me, thinking that our work is fruitless, ﴿then indeed we ridicule﴾, that is, we bring about ridicule ﴿of you﴾ as recompense for you ﴿as you ridicule﴾ us now, because our work brings salvation, and your work is not limited to loss but rather necessitates what you are threatened with of punishment. So it is you who will be disgraced, not I." Since His saying ﴿we ridicule of you﴾ stands in the place of this announcement, the use of the particle "fa" (then), which signals that the aforementioned knowledge is a consequence of it, is apt, in His saying: ﴿so you will know﴾, that is, by a promise that admits no failure, (p-285) ﴿who will receive a punishment that disgraces him﴾, that is, that exposes him and so humiliates him. It seems that by this is meant the punishment of this world. ﴿And there will descend upon him﴾, that is, descent like that of a debt from which there is no escape, ﴿a lasting punishment﴾, and this is the punishment of the Hereafter. Something similar has passed in Surat al-An'am at His saying: ﴿So you will know for whom will be the final outcome of the abode﴾ [al-An'am 6:135]. And ridicule (suKhriyya) is the display of what contradicts what is concealed, in a manner intended to make one understand the weakness of intellect, from taskhir, which is subjugation, humbling through overpowering weakness. It differs from play (la'ib) in that it involves a deception that provokes agitation, so it is not found except with a living being, whereas play may occur with an inanimate object, since it is simply the seeking of joy. And disgrace (khizy) is the defect whose exposure is evident and the shame attached to it; its counterpart is humiliation and degradation. This remained their custom and his custom. ﴿Until when Our command came﴾, that is, the time of Our will to destroy them, ﴿and the tannur boiled over﴾, that is, it became hot and overflowed. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and from al-Hasan and Mujahid, that it is the literal oven in which bread is baked. This is the apparent meaning, so one does not turn from it except by evidence, because diverting a word from its apparent meaning without evidence is futile, as the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (ahl al-usul) have said. ﴿We said﴾, by Our majesty: ﴿Carry﴾ [Since God had commanded him to make a covering for it, as the exegetes have said, so that it would not be filled by the severity of the rains, the containing sense of "in it" was clear in this case unlike other ships; therefore He said]: ﴿in it﴾, that is, the ship, ﴿from every pair of two﴾ of the animals. The "pair" (zawj) is a single which has another with it, whose benefit is not complete except with it, ﴿two﴾, male and female. ﴿And your family﴾, that is, carry them. The "family" (ahl) means the dependents, (p-286) ﴿except him against whom the word has already preceded﴾, that is, the one for whom it has been decided, by My saying that I will drown him, and he was his wife and his son Kan'an. ﴿And whoever believed﴾, that is, and carry in it whoever believed. Abu Hayyan said: The ship had three decks: the lowest for the wild animals, the middle for food and drink, and the highest for him and those who believed with him. Then He consoled the addressee of these stories, ﷺ, and reminded him of His blessing by the large number of those who followed him, despite their turning away from the painful warning, over a short time, unlike Nuh, upon them be peace, despite the long duration. So He said: ﴿And there believed with him﴾, that is, while the situation was that there believed with him, in response to his warning, ﴿only a few﴾, by reason of Our decree, not by their indifference despite the warning they were met with. As for "tannur": Abu Hayyan said: its form is fa'ul according to Abu 'Ali, and it is non-Arabic. Tha'lab said: its form is taf'ul from al-nur (light), and its origin is tannur, the waw was hamzated then lightened, and the letter preceding it was doubled. As for "zawj" (pair), it has been used widely for a man who has a wife. Al-Rummani said: al-Hasan said concerning His saying ﴿And of everything We created pairs﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:49]: the heaven is a pair, the earth is a pair, winter is a pair, summer is a pair, night is a pair, day is a pair, until the matter returns to God, the One who is unique, to whom nothing is like. The meaning of this is in Sahih al-Bukhari. The least that has been said of those who were in the ship is eight: Nuh, his wife, and three sons: Sam, Ham, and Yafith, and their wives. The most that has been said is that they were eighty, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father.
