(p-313) When he had completed his building up of the argument and refuted their claims, he began to warn them, explaining that turning away from what he brought can only come from treating the sound disposition (al-ṭab' al-salīm, natural human disposition) in a particular way: ﴿But if you turn away﴾, even with the slightest turning away, as indicated by the omission of the *tā'* (in the original reading, the second *tā'* of *tatawallaw* is elided), then the blame falls on you and not on me, because I have done what was incumbent upon me. ﴿Then I have indeed conveyed to you what﴾, that is, because I have already, ﴿I was sent with﴾, that is, my sending has preceded from the One from whom there is no true sender but Him, ﴿to you﴾, in full, leaving nothing out of it, hoping for your acceptance or fearing your rejection. But you refused except to deny me and to be arrogant toward what I brought. So the One who sent me will take vengeance on you and destroy you. ﴿And my Lord will replace﴾, that is, will bring into being, He who has been good to me by enabling me to act in what pleases Him, ﴿a people other than you﴾, who will succeed you in your homes and your possessions, so that you will become His enemies, and those who are substituted will be exposed to becoming allies [despite being people of might and strength], so the harm will fall specifically upon you. ﴿And you will not harm Him﴾, that is, God, by your turning away, ﴿in the least.﴾ Then he gave the reason for his threat to them with his statement, emphasized because the disobedient one acts through his disobedience as one who thinks that God is heedless of him: ﴿Indeed, my Lord﴾, that is, the One who has been good to me, who manages my interests.

Since the more important matter in this context is to show His supremacy and power, he placed before the phrase ﴿over everything﴾, whether small or great, noble or base, ﴿is Guardian﴾, that is, knowing of everything, able over everything, and [and] of perfect preservation of it. He knows what the preserved thing does, and so He will repay it with what it deserves of His bounties and His retributions. This is therefore an explanation for the substitution of others in their place and for His exemption from being harmed. For *al-ḥifẓ* (preservation, guarding) means watchful protection, which entails knowledge and power. From power comes *ḥāfiẓ al-ʿayn* (one who keeps the eye watchful), that is, one whom sleep does not overcome. *Al-ḥafīẓah* (zeal, anger) relates to protective pride and wrath, and from both together comes *al-muḥāfaẓah* (perseverance), meaning constancy in something. *Al-tawallī ʿan al-shayʾ* (turning away from something) means going in a direction other than its own, turning aside from it. *Al-iblāgh* (conveying) means bringing a thing to its ultimate end. *Al-istikhlāf* (substitution) means making a second thing a replacement for the first, standing in its place. *Al-ḍurr* (harm) means causing pain, either by the act itself or by being its cause.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 58:

When this was complete, it was as if it had been said: they did not turn back, nor did they heed, neither for a clear sign, nor out of desire, nor out of fear; so We sent down upon them Our command. ﴿And when Our command came﴾, that is, the time of Our will to destroy ʿAd, ﴿We delivered﴾, that is, a great deliverance befitting what We possess of greatness, ﴿Hud and those who believed﴾ along with him, ﴿with him﴾ in faith and in deliverance from their people. They were unable to reach them with harm, despite their striving in that and their pride in their strength. It is said that those who believed were four thousand.

Since He, glory be to Him, is such that nothing is owed to anyone from Him, for no one can measure Him as He deserves however much he strives in obedience to Him, and since obedience to Him is itself a blessing from Him upon the one who obeys, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾, confirming the trust of Our servant. Having explained their deliverance from their people, He explained their deliverance from what He destroyed them with, saying [repeating the mention of deliverance to show that their punishment was at the utmost of severity]: ﴿And We delivered them﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness. He explained the severity of what He destroyed their enemies with by His saying: ﴿from a harsh punishment﴾, that is, We destroyed their opponents with it, and it is the violent wind (al-rīḥ al-ṣarṣar). This is preferable to taking it as the punishment of the Hereafter, because of His saying later: ﴿and from disgrace on that day﴾ [Hud: 66]. It is as though, when they saw signs of the punishment, they set out against their prophet and those who believed with him to destroy them before they themselves were destroyed, as was explicitly stated in the story of Salih. Najat (deliverance) is safety from destruction. The literal meaning of ghilẓah (harshness) is the largeness of a body, and it was borrowed for punishment because of its weight upon the soul and the length of its duration.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 59:

When their story had been completed in this wondrous manner and eloquent, captivating style, God the Exalted said, linking it to His words ﴿That is from the news of the unseen﴾ [Hud: 49]: ﴿And that was ʿAd﴾, i.e., the story of the people who were far removed (from good) and full of hatred, which you did not know in this detail, neither you nor your people nor the People of the Book. The People of the Book were mentioned as not knowing it only because they do not know anything except what has a basis in the reports of their prophets. This story and the story of Thamud are not in the Torah, nor in any of the books of their prophets. I asked some of their scholars and did not find with them any knowledge of it, not a single letter, and they had not heard of ʿAd or Hud.

The summary of their story is that they ﴿denied﴾, i.e., they rejected out of obstinacy and contempt, ﴿the signs of their Lord﴾, the One who was good to them, ﴿and disobeyed His messengers﴾. Whoever disobeyed one of them has disobeyed all of them, since they agreed upon one matter, equal in the absolute nature of the miracle. ﴿And they followed﴾, i.e., with the utmost of their effort, ﴿the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾, i.e., an overpowering oppressor of extreme domination who compels others to do what he wills. This indicates that there is no excuse in the basic matter of religion in any way, for the inner states of hearts are known only to God [so it is possible for everyone to oppose the tyrant in this]. ﴿Obstinate﴾, i.e., a transgressing rebel who does not accept the truth in any way. So they were destroyed, and their tyranny did not protect them, nor did their obstinacy and arrogance avail them.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 11, verse 60:**

﴿And they were followed﴾ all together, after their destruction, in the easiest manner, indicating the great power of the One who follows up on them. ﴿In this world﴾: He belittled it in this expression by means of the demonstrative, which points to it, together with the diminutive form, and by what indicates its nearness. It also indicates that whoever is deceived by it is among those who stop at the visible, because of its rigidity (*judud*). ﴿A curse﴾, that is, expulsion, distance, and destruction. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that is, likewise, or rather worse. It is as if it were said: "Is there then no loss for their calamity?" So it was said: "No." The *alā* (ألا, "unquestionably") opens the announcement about them with this particle, which is used only before a statement of great weight and great importance. The emphasis in the announcement of their disbelief establishes their state. Among the proofs of prophethood and signs of the message is the refutation of a group that has appeared near our time, who deem all religions correct. They single out this people of ʿAd because they are the most self-satisfied of them, saying that they are among those brought near to God and that they are under His gaze of approval. So God is asked to grant victory over them and to heal the hearts of the believers from them. They are the followers of Ibn ʿArabi, the stubborn unbeliever, the people of *ittihad* (the doctrine of the unity of being), who openly profess great impiety and treat the Lord of the servants with contempt. Therefore God, the Exalted, said, explaining their state with an explanation that leaves no ambiguity: ﴿Indeed, ʿAd disbelieved﴾. He did not limit the verb but made it transitive, magnifying their rebellion, and said: ﴿their Lord﴾, that is, they covered over [all the lights of] the manifest, whose concealment is not valid at all, because there is no blessing upon any creature except from Him. [So their disbelief was the grossest disbelief. Yet Hud, peace be upon him, did not desist from conveying to them everything he was commanded, nor did he omit anything that was revealed to him. For you there is a good example in him, and in them a warning.] Whoever disbelieves in one to whom he has shown kindness has gone a distance with no nearness in it.

Since the matter was great and the affair momentous, he repeated the particle used for weighty matters and said: ﴿Unquestionably, a distance for ʿAd﴾, [it is] from *baʿida* (بَعِدَ, with the vowel of the ʿayn in kasra) when its distance is by destruction. He specified them by saying: ﴿the people of Hud﴾, to establish them clearly, since they were two ʿAds: the first and the last. It also hints that their deserving of being removed from mercy is due to what happened to Hud, peace be upon him, with them, namely their denial and his invocation against them after their destruction, as an allusion to the report that they were deserving of destruction. Al-jahd (denial) is the report about something whose truth is known, that one does not know it; it is the opposite of acknowledgment, just as negation is the opposite of affirmation. Thus it is a report merely by absence, and so it is more general. Al-ʿisyan (disobedience) is the opposite of what the caller was commanded to do in the manner of obligation. Al-laʿna (the curse) is the supplication for distance, and its origin is distance from good. Al-itbaʿ (following up) is placing the second upon the trace of the first; al-iblagh (conveying) is more specific than it. What is meant here is its reaching them, because He who decreed this is capable, and He has overtaken them with the punishment of this world, which removes them from the places of mercy.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 61:

When the story of ʿAd had ended as He willed, He followed it with the story of those who came after them in time and were similar to them in dwelling in the land of the Arabs and in worshipping idols. The connection lies in the matter of the punishment: the means by which the Cry reached the ears is the wind (p-318), and the matter of their concealment, [being] detailed for the people of that time. So He said: ﴿And to﴾, meaning: And indeed We sent to ﴿Thamud their brother﴾, and He specified him with His words: ﴿Salih﴾. Then He presented his speech ﷺ as if in answer to a question, and said: ﴿He said: "O my people"﴾, meaning: O you whom it grieves me that any evil should befall them, ﴿worship Allah﴾, meaning the Greatest King alone, because your worship of Him alongside another is worth nothing. Then he began to explain that, and said: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾. He went to the extreme in negation and said: ﴿other than Him﴾, following the method of those who call to Allah regarding the foundation of the religion, which is singling out the Benefactor for worship.

When he had commanded them to this, he reminded them of His power and favour, encouraging and warning, and said: ﴿He it is who produced you﴾, meaning: He alone, ﴿from the earth﴾ meaning He began your creation, by creating Adam, peace be upon him, from it without an intermediary, and by creating you from the seminal fluid [from the blood], which comes from food, which comes from plants, which come from the earth, just as He produced your idols from it. ﴿And﴾ He elevated your standing upon it by ﴿making you its inhabitants﴾, meaning He qualified you for what He did not qualify the idols for, namely that you be its cultivators ﴿therein﴾. So do not forget the right of your God and what He has favoured you with, of the right of your own selves, by submitting to what is not equal to you; how then [should you submit] to One who produced you and it? And "production" (inshaʾ) means initiating existence without seeking help from any of the causes.

When He, glory be to Him, had made His greatness clear to them, and Satan had confused them by suggesting to them that the idols were intercessors (p-319), [and since He, by His greatness, cannot be reached by any means, as is the case with kings], He negated that, explaining the way of return to Him by His words: ﴿So seek forgiveness from Him﴾, meaning: turn to Him with all your hearts, seeking that He conceal your sins. He mentioned the condition of forgiveness with His words, indicating with the particle of distance the greatness of the station: ﴿Then repent﴾, meaning: return with all your hearts ﴿to Him﴾. Then He gave the reason for that by His kindness and tenderness, encouraging turning towards Him, and He said, emphasising, because whoever sees His respite to the disobedient will entertain suspicions, and whoever disobeys Him acts like one who denies His nearness and His answering: ﴿Indeed my Lord﴾, to whom I have made my worship sincere for His goodness to me, and I call you to sincerity towards Him for His goodness to you, ﴿is near﴾ to everyone who turns to Him, without need of toil in walking or bodily movement, ﴿and answering﴾ to everyone who calls upon Him, unlike your worshipped things in both respects together.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 62:

When he (Salih) called them to the truth, and set before them the proofs (adillah) of it, of which they were themselves aware, and reminded them of His blessings while alluding to the warning against His retribution, and made the path to reaching Him easy for them, their response was nothing but to strip him of the stage of humanity for the sake of pure imitation (taqlid). Therefore He resumed the report of their answer with His words: ﴿They said﴾, i.e., Thamud, ﴿O Salih﴾, they called him by his name, out of lack of courtesy (adab) and coarseness on their part, ﴿you were among us﴾, i.e., among us when we discussed your affair, ﴿a hope﴾, i.e., within the category of those in whom it is right to hope that there would be good, nobility (su'dud), guidance (rushd) and righteousness. They covered all of time, so they omitted the preposition and said: ﴿before this﴾, i.e., before what you have called us to. As for after this, you have departed from that category. Then they made clear what caused his fall in their eyes, saying, denying with the denial of one who is burnt (mu'tariq): ﴿Do you forbid us﴾, i.e., an absolute prohibition, ﴿from worshipping﴾, i.e., perpetually, ﴿what our fathers worshipped﴾. They expressed it in the present tense (sighat al-mudari') to depict the present state, as if their fathers were still living, so opposing them is not possible out of reverence for them. Thus they venerated one whom they saw as the near cause of their existence, and did not revere the One who originated them and their fathers, first from the earth and then from sperm-drops. Then He bestowed upon them what they had. Then, regarding the foundation of the religion, after mentioning what drove them to disbelief, which prevented them from abandoning it, they resorted to bluster, claiming that what necessitates certainty for every intelligent person from His manifest sign had not affected them except with something below conjecture as a reason for refusing to respond to him. So they said, emphasizing (because their doubt deserves to be denied, since it concerns a matter that is very clear and admits no doubt at all): ﴿Indeed we are in doubt﴾, [and] they added emphasis with the nun and lam, and with the expression of the adverbial phrase indicating that doubt encompasses them, ﴿concerning﴾. Since the one calling them was single, namely Salih, peace be upon him, they attached to the verb only one nun, which is their pronoun, unlike what occurs in Surat Ibrahim, peace be upon him, so they said: ﴿that to which you invite us﴾, i.e., the worship of God alone, ﴿disquieting﴾, i.e., causing unease, which is the restlessness of the soul and the absence of tranquility through certainty. Al-raja' (hope) is the soul's attachment to the coming of good by way of conjecture; its counterparts are al-amal (expectation) and al-tama' (desire). Al-nahy (prohibition) is the restraint from an act by the form "do not do."

(p-321) When they presented their matter to him in the form of doubt while intending certainty, he met them with its like in the form of supposition [out of fairness to them, so that the address would not be unsuited to the state of those addressed]. So God, glory be to Him, resumed reporting about him in His words: ﴿He said﴾, i.e., Salih, calling them gently to consider his matter: ﴿O my people, tell me﴾, i.e., inform me ﴿if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord﴾, he stated it in the form of doubt because his address was to the deniers. ﴿From my Lord﴾, i.e., the One who has been good to me, about which I have no doubt ﴿and He has given me mercy from Him﴾, i.e., commands which are a cause of mercy. ﴿Then who will support me against Allah﴾. He placed the explicit noun in place of the pronoun and used the Greatest Name because the context calls for awe, so he said: ﴿against Allah﴾, i.e., the Supreme King ﴿if I disobey Him﴾, i.e., your falling into doubt [according to your claim] has led you to a posture of refusal in engaging in their deeds, despite their vanishing and perishing; if they were existent and you disobeyed them, you would not care about them. As for me, the One whom He commanded me to worship is living and capable of recompensing whoever obeys Him or disobeys Him, and the least that impels one to obey Him is doubt about His punishment, which suffices the sensible person in avoiding danger. ﴿So you add to me﴾, i.e., as a consequence of your forbidding me to call to Him, glory be to Him, you add to me nothing by this ﴿except loss﴾ in my work by what you accuse me of, namely turning away from Him by following you in your deeds, or refraining from you so that I would be counted among those hoped for by you as possessing intellect; ﴿except loss﴾, i.e., bringing me into ruin on this assumption. So do not hope that I will abandon any of my opposition to you as long as you remain (p-322) in your present state. The verse, as you see, looks toward His words, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you would leave some of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud: 12].

O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah (Allah being al-Malik al-A'la, the Supreme King), as a sign for you. Ibn al-Biqa'i's point here: Allah brought her forth for them from the rock, in the presence of those who witnessed it. The phrase ﴿lakum﴾ means specifically for you, for your looking at her when she came out, and for everyone who hears of her after you; but the report is not like direct witnessing.

Ibn al-Biqa'i says that the phrase ﴿ayatan﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) placed before its governing element so that it would not be a qualifier (ṣifah) of her. The sign is shown by the fact that Allah brought her out for you from a rock, while she was pregnant (ʿushharāʾ), according to what you proposed, while you were watching. Another sign is that she has a share of drinking on one day, while you each have a share of drinking on one day; she has a share of grazing on one day, while all your animals and the wild beasts of your lands share grazing on one day; and so on, of what you see and know.

﴿So leave her﴾, meaning leave her in whatever state your leaving her may be, ﴿to eat﴾ [meaning, of what she wishes] ﴿in the earth of Allah﴾, meaning the King to whom all command belongs, which He created from it, ﴿and do not touch her with harm﴾. Al-akl (eating) is chewing that occurs before swallowing; al-mass (touching) is general contact and can occur between an animal and other things, while al-lams (feeling) is more specific than it, because it involves perception (p. 323) ﴿so that a painful punishment will seize you﴾, meaning: as a consequence of that, a punishment will seize you ﴿soon﴾, meaning: from the time you harm her.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 65:

Then he indicated how close they were to defying his command concerning her, by His saying, as a consequence of and following upon His commands and prohibitions: ﴿But they hamstrung her﴾, i.e., the she-camel. ﴿So he said﴾, i.e., [when] his message reached them: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your home﴾, i.e., [you] will live in your home, ﴿for three days﴾, i.e., without any addition to them. So consider what your pleasure and luxury will avail you, even if you strive for it.

Since it was as though it were said: "Is there any alternative to this threat?" he answered, saying: ﴿That is﴾, i.e., this promise, lofty in rank in truth and in wrath, ﴿a promise not to be denied﴾, i.e., it will certainly come to pass. And tamattu' (enjoyment): the taking of pleasure in pleasant perceptible things, such as sights, sounds and other things perceived by the senses. The lands were called dar (home) because they gather their people together, as a house gathers them, and because they are circulated (yuddaru) within them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 66:

He indicated the following of the punishment upon the days and its being a consequence of the specified threat, by His saying: ﴿So when Our command came﴾ with the letter fa' (so, meaning immediate sequence), unlike what is in the story of Hud and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them both. That is: with the passing of the days, the first thing We did was ﴿deliver﴾, by Our might and greatness, Our allies ﴿Salih and those who believed with him﴾ from the plot of their people. [And He made clear that His beneficence, glory be to Him, is only out of His bounty, by His saying]: ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾. This is because he, peace be upon him, said to them: "You will rise tomorrow, a day of cheerfulness" - meaning Thursday - "and your faces will be yellow. Then you will rise on a day of 'uruba" - meaning Friday - "and your faces will be red. Then you will rise on a day of shiyar and your faces will be black. Then the punishment will seize you at dawn on the day of awwal" - that is, Sunday. The nine men of the group who hamstrung the she-camel said: "Come, let us kill Salih. If he is truthful, we will hasten him before us, and if he is lying, we will have joined him to his she-camel." So they came to him at night to ambush him in his family, but the angels struck them with stones. When they were slow in returning to their companions, they came to the dwelling of Salih and found them crushed by stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them!" Then they intended to attack him, but his clan stood between them and him, put on their weapons, and said to them: "By God, you shall never kill him, for he has promised you that the punishment will befall you after three days. If he is truthful, you will only increase your Lord's wrath upon you, and if he is lying, you are beyond what you desire." So they withdrew. When their faces became yellow in the morning, they knew that he had spoken the truth, so they sought him to kill him. He came to a clan of theirs called (Banu Ghanm), and he descended upon their chief [a man], and he hid him with him. They then attacked the companions of Salih, torturing them in order to lead them to him. They said: "O Prophet of God! They are torturing us so that we will guide them to you; shall we guide them?" He said: (p-325) "Yes." So they guided them to him, and they came to him, and the Ghanmi said: "Yes, he is with me, but there is no way to him." So they left him, and what God sent down upon them occupied them from him. [Thus] al-Baghawi related this from Ibn Ishaq, Wahb, and others, at length.

When He mentioned their deliverance from every destruction, He mentioned their deliverance from the specific thing by which their people were punished, and said: ﴿And from disgrace﴾, that is: and We delivered them from ﴿disgrace﴾, meaning humiliation and exposure, ﴿on that day﴾, that is: the day when Our command came to destroy them with the Blast, and it descended upon them, distinguishing between Our allies and Our enemies. [The omission of "We delivered" here indicates that their punishment was less than the punishment of 'Ad]. Then He followed this with its causal explanation, both the destruction and the deliverance, by His being characterized by the attributes of subjugation, dominance, and retribution, and said: ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you just as He was good to the prophets before you, ﴿He is﴾, that is: alone, ﴿the Strong﴾, so He overcomes everything, ﴿the Mighty﴾, that is, the one able to prevent others without anyone being able to overpower Him or to resist Him, from 'azza al-shay', meaning it became unassailable; from it comes 'izaz, for hard ground that resists being worked by that. And khizy: the defect whose disgrace becomes manifest and at which one is ashamed before its like.

Then he explained His descent upon their enemies after He had delivered His allies, saying, exalting the seizing by the masculine form of the verb: ﴿And the cry seized those who had done wrong﴾. He indicated the magnitude of this cry (p-326) by dropping the feminine marker, and he made the following statement its consequence: ﴿So they became prostrate in their homes﴾, i.e., fallen upon their faces. It was also said: crouching on their knees, dead, with no movement in them. The reason for the expression "homes" (diyar) with the cry, and "abode" (dar) with the quake, was discussed earlier in al-A'raf. Hud is singled out for what is mentioned in it, because its purpose is more concerned with detail, and both "homes" and "cry" are closer to that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 68:

Since crouching (al-juthum) is a metaphor for death, he made it clear by his saying: ﴿As if﴾, that is, as if they ﴿had not flourished﴾, that is, had not dwelt as wealthy people, enjoying themselves ﴿therein﴾. Then he drew attention to what they deserved for this, for the one who might be heedless and ask, by his saying, opening with the particle that is used only with momentous matters: ﴿Indeed, Thamud﴾. The reading with tanwin (ṣarf) indicates contempt for them [because of their recklessness in disobedience] ﴿disbelieved in their Lord﴾, that is, they cast a covering and concealment over the One who did good to them by creating them, providing for them, and sending to them, which is the apparent meaning, and over His attributes and actions, so that it is not hidden from anyone at all. [Thus the verb is stated without restriction, as in most of its like, as a clarification of the severity of their disbelief]. Then he repeated that as emphasis for it and as an announcement of the perpetuity of their destruction by his saying: ﴿Indeed, remoteness to Thamud!﴾ He left their tanwin unpronounced in the reading other than that of al-Kisa'i, as an indication of the lasting of their stay in expulsion and distance. The Sayhah (blast) is a great sound from the mouth of a living being, and al-juthum is for the persistence in one place, or falling upon the face; it was said also: sitting on the knees. He said: ﴿they became﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 102], as an increase in the warning and the regret over what befell them of loss, which would be felt if any one of them had lived to see it, because a person rejoices when he rises in the morning from his sleep, rested and able to make the movements he wants, to enjoy what he desires of activities. So these people, after this description as Allah recounted, became extinguished all together like a single soul, men and women, young and old, as if they had never existed [at all, nor did they produce any separation or connection, as if they had never existed], a coolness to the eyes, nor were they counted among the living even once, "as if they had not flourished"; that is, they did not dwell, because their traces were cut off, except for what remained of their bodies, which indicate the disgrace. Al-maghani: the dwellings. The root of ghana is sufficiency. The meaning of "alā" is alerting. Al-Rummani said: it is the interrogative alif that entered upon "lā"; the alif requires a meaning, and "lā" negates a meaning, so the speech with both implies the meaning of alerting together with negating heedlessness, end of quote.

But its reality, and Allah knows best, is that "lā" entered upon what follows it and negated it, then the interrogative hamzah entered upon it and negated it, and it is known that negating a negation is an affirmation, so the meaning returned as it was, in the most complete forms of alerting and emphasis; because affirming a meaning after negating it is more emphatic than affirming it bare of negation, especially when the one conveying that is the denial. This meaning applies consistently to the accidental "alā" and the restrictive "halā" and the like, and it runs in every connective by returning it to the root of its signification in the language and then using it as the situation requires. And Allah is the Guide.

Since the tanwin in Thamud was permissible on account of it being the name of the tribe's father, and its absence on account of its use for the tribe, the tanwin was chosen in the accusative case only, for its lightness.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 69:

When the story was concluded in this marvelous manner, he followed it with the story of Lot, peace be upon him, since it was the most famous of the events after it, and it is more dreadful and more awe-inspiring. He placed before it what is connected with it concerning the affair of Abraham, peace be upon him, and mentioned his good tidings, because in all of that there is an admonition for whoever insolently demanded the sending down of angels, in their saying: ﴿Or an angel should accompany him﴾ [Hud: 12], indicating that this is not difficult for Him. He has done it often, but their descent is frightening, and their appearance in plain view is terrifying, whereas when they are concealed it does not cut off their insolence. Along with this, there is the correspondence between the affair of this son and the affair of the she-camel, in that each of them was brought into being in a manner that breaks the usual custom, as a sign of the completeness of power and the perfection of knowledge, on which the affair of the surah is based, in the perfection of the Book and its detailing. There is also the correspondence between the disputes of Noah and Abraham, peace be upon them both, in that each of them was a compassionate concern for the disbelievers and a hope for their salvation from punishment through a good return. Perhaps He, glory be to Him, repeated "la-qad" (indeed) at its beginning, in conformity with what is in the story of Noah, to alert to similar purposes, because "qad" indicates anticipation, so it came to inform that the listener is in a state of anticipation for that. For when the story of the report concerning what follows it has concluded, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed﴾. Al-Rummani said: The lam entered to emphasize the report, just as an oath emphasizes. ﴿Our messengers came﴾, meaning those whose greatness derives from our greatness; it is said they were Gabriel, Michael and Israfil, peace be upon them. ﴿To Abraham﴾, who is the Friend of Allah, peace be upon him, ﴿with the good tidings﴾, meaning those which are among the greatest of glad tidings, and they were his honoring with Isaac, peace be upon him, as a son to him from his wife Sarah, may Allah be pleased with her. [They came to him] in the form he loves, which is the form of guests. So he did not recognize them, although he was the Friend, but rather he disowned them, as He, exalted is He, said in adh-Dhariyat: ﴿He said: Peace. A people unknown﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 25]. Thus his disowning them at first is understood as astonishment, meaning that he did not see upon them the dress of the people of that land nor any trace of travel. So it is as if it were said: What was their matter? Then it was said: ﴿They said: Peace﴾, meaning: We greeted you with a great greeting. ﴿He said: Peace﴾, meaning: a lasting, enduring peace upon you that never ceases. The nominative has a distinction over the accusative, because it is a report about something fixed, whereas the accusative is a renewal of what was not. So it fell under ﴿Then greet with something better than it﴾ [an-Nisa: 86]. Then he honored their hospitality and set about doing what Allah had given him of noble dispositions and the deeds of the generous in the etiquette of hospitality, such as hastening together with excellence. ﴿And he did not delay﴾, meaning: [as a consequence of their coming and following it], he did not delay ﴿to bring a roasted calf﴾, meaning: roasted on hot stones in a trench, [and above it hot stones so that its cooking would be thorough], so after roasting it was dripping its fat, because it was fat. All of this while he did not know they were angels; rather he was certain they were among those who eat. This looks to the saying of the people of Noah (p-330): ﴿We see you have no superiority over us﴾ [Hud: 27] and His saying: ﴿Nor do I say to those whom your eyes look down upon﴾ [Hud: 31], to the end of the verse. That is, Allah placed meanings in the hearts and attached happiness and misery to them, and those meanings may be hidden, just as it was hidden from the most perfect people of that time that his guests were angels, to the point that he feared them, although they had brought him good tidings. So no one should belittle anyone except in what Allah has permitted.

When he set the food before them, they did not reach out to it. ﴿So when he saw their hands not reaching toward it﴾, that is, the messengers' hands, [immediately after it was set down], ﴿not reaching toward it﴾, that is, toward the calf he had placed for them to eat, ﴿he felt strange toward them﴾. That is, his strangeness toward them became intense, and he was affected by it. This indicates what some scholars have said: that *nakira* (نَكِرَ) is more emphatic than *ankara* (أنْكَرَ). ﴿And he sensed fear of them in his heart﴾, that is, he concealed it inwardly in his heart, ﴿a fear [that was great]﴾, because of what he saw of their conditions and witnessed of their majesty. [The root meaning of *wujūs* (وُجُوس) is entry.] The evidence that his fear was due to his knowledge through *tawassum* (discernment by outward signs), that they were angels who had descended on a matter he disliked, such as punishing one who was dear to him, or something similar, is that ﴿they said, "Do not fear"﴾. Then they gave the reason for this in their words, ﴿"Indeed, we have been sent"﴾, that is, by one whose command cannot be turned back, ﴿"to the people of Lot."﴾ They removed his fear by informing him of the people to whom they had been sent, not by saying that they were angels. They said this and gave him the good news of a son.

[Their messengers had come to him with the good news, meaning they had told him of it], and his wife, who was of complete dignity, namely Sarah, was **standing**. It has been said that she was standing at the door of the tent, perhaps so that she might gain some help in serving them. She heard the good news of a son, which was indicated earlier by His saying: ﴿with the good news﴾ [Hud 69]. ﴿So she laughed﴾, meaning she marvelled at that good news for her husband, despite his old age. Perhaps she thought it came from someone other than him, because although she was barren, she was an old woman. This is the use of the effect (al-musabbab) to denote the cause (al-sabab), [indicating that her wonder was great]. ﴿Then We gave her good news﴾, meaning her wonder led to Our renewing the good news for her directly, through the tongue of the angels, as an honour to her and to confirm that it would come from her: ﴿of Isaac﴾, whom she would bear, ﴿and after Isaac, Jacob﴾, meaning that Jacob would be a son of Isaac. What indicates what I have determined, that they gave the good news to him of the son before his wife, and she heard and wondered, is what comes from the text of the Tawrah (Torah), and the just judge over all of that is His saying, Exalted is He, in al-Dhariyat: ﴿They said, "Fear not," and gave him good news of a knowing boy﴾ [al-Dhariyat 28], ﴿Then his wife came forward in a loud cry and slapped her face﴾ [al-Dhariyat 29], and so on.

When they addressed her with this, she voiced her astonishment at the fact that he was combining two wonders, in that he was from them and from her, by saying, ﴿Woe to me!﴾ This is an expression that signals a terrible matter, and it is light on the tongues of women, who still use it to this day, though they have altered its wording, as much speech has been altered. Al-wayl (ruin, woe) means the descent of evil. The alif at its end (الألف) is a replacement for the ya' of possession (ياء الإضافة). Here it is used as a metonymy for intense wonder, because of the fame attached to it and the crowding of doubts. Al-Rummani said: its meaning is an announcement of the arrival of a terrible matter, as the Arabs say, "Ya lil-dawahi!" (O calamities!), meaning, "Come, for this is one of your times, so the presence of what has come is among your kinds of events."

Since what she had been given good news of was, in itself, unusual according to custom, she said, ﴿Shall I bear a child when I am an old woman and this is my husband, an old man?﴾ That is, while the situation is that I am an old woman, and this one who is present with me is my husband, an old man. Then she expressed that by its result, saying [emphasizing, because it is, by virtue of its breaking of customary patterns, within the scope of what is unusual in people's eyes]: ﴿Indeed, this is truly a wonderful thing.﴾ That is, the matter that was announced. It is as if it was said: "What did they say to her then?" So it was said: ﴿They said﴾, that is, the angels, marvelling at her marvelling, ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah?﴾ That is, the One to whom all perfection belongs. It is not fitting for you, because you are accustomed to receiving from Allah what is not granted to others, of extraordinary events. Wonder arises only from what departs from its usual forms and whose cause is hidden, whereas you, because your knowledge of the cause, which is Allah's power over everything, is firm, and His presence is with you, together with Allah's choosing of you and the repeated breaking of customs in your affairs, are not like others who lack this. Then they gave as the reason for their denial of her wonder, by saying, ﴿The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of this house.﴾ That is, the honour of the One who encompasses the attributes of majesty and generosity, and His blessings, that is, His goodness, which grows and is firmly established, upon you. They made clear their particularity by omitting the particle of address [as praise for them], so He said: ﴿O people of the house.﴾ You have been trained to witness wonders, because of how much you see of His effects, such as this and others. [Then He gave the reason for His beneficence toward them, emphasizing it to confirm the basis of the speech which she had denied, so He said]: ﴿Indeed, He﴾, that is, with regard to this particular beneficence, ﴿is Praiseworthy, Glorious﴾ [meaning] abundant in making Himself known to whomever He wills of sublime favours and great capacity, by which it is recognized that He deserves praise for glory, and this is the generosity from which bounty arises.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 74–75:

When they had heard that and become reassured, he proceeded to narrate what came after it, and said, using the particle "fa" (fa, "then") to indicate the brevity of the period of disapproval, which was the cause of the fear: ﴿So when the fright had left Abraham﴾ with the matter being revealed, ﴿and the good tidings had come to him﴾ so that he was filled with joy. ﴿He began to dispute with Us﴾, meaning: he began to act toward Us by disputing with Our messengers, in the manner of one who disputes and whose speech multiplies, desiring to turn his interlocutor away from what he says, ﴿concerning the people of Lot﴾, meaning: he asked Us about their deliverance with a question in which he eagerly strove, as the disputant strives to turn something aside. "Jidal" (jidal, disputation) comes from "jadl," which means twisting. He placed the present tense (yujadilunā) in the place of the past to indicate the repetition of the dispute while depicting the situation, meaning: he disputed with Us about them at length. Then he gave the reason for his dispute with His words: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing﴾, meaning: he was eloquent in ḥilm (ḥilm, forbearance), which is granting respite to the one guilty of a sin as reason requires; ﴿grieving much﴾, meaning: one who often sighs out of fear of falling short; ﴿and turning back (to Allah)﴾, meaning: one who often returns to Allah by being foremost in ascending the stages of nearness. Thus, because he possesses these virtues, he never ceases to hope for the desisting of the disobedient.

Then he gave the reason for his dispute with His words: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing﴾, meaning: he was eloquent in ḥilm (ḥilm, forbearance), which is granting respite to the one guilty of a sin as reason requires; ﴿grieving much﴾, meaning: one who often sighs out of fear of falling short; ﴿and turning back (to Allah)﴾, meaning: one who often returns to Allah by being foremost in ascending the stages of nearness. Thus, because he possesses these virtues, he never ceases to hope for the desisting of the disobedient.

(p-334) Since most of the disputing came from his compassion for God's servants, because of these noble attributes he had, God informed him that the matter had been concluded with His saying, as a narration, that after long disputing the messengers said to him, addressing him with the particle that is the "mother of the chapter" (umm al-bab), to announce that what follows is of great importance and high station: ﴿O Abraham, turn away from this﴾, meaning, entirely, ﴿from this﴾, meaning the request concerning their deliverance. He then gave the reason for this, emphasized, because his disputing was within the category of one who denies the finality of the matter: ﴿Indeed, it has come﴾, opened with the particle of expectation (tawaqquʿ, anticipation of an event), since that is its proper place, ﴿the command of your Lord﴾, meaning the One who accustomed you to His abundant kindness. Had He not decreed the matter, with their punishment, He would have granted them respite for your sake. Therefore he linked to the reason his emphasized statement, to announce that it is a matter that has been settled and has passed: ﴿and indeed there will come upon them﴾, meaning, a certain coming, ﴿a punishment that cannot be turned back﴾, meaning, in any way, from anyone, whoever he may be. Al-Iʿrāḍ (إعْراضُ, turning away) is departure, and its reality is going away from a thing in the direction of its breadth. Al-Radd (الرَّدُّ, turning back) is returning a thing to where it came from, like a return. Al-Daf‘ (الدَّفْعُ, repelling) is more general, since it may be toward the front. When he knew God's intention regarding them, he placed it before his own intention and did not utter a word after that.

The mention of this story from the Torah: In the First Book it says: "And God appeared to Abraham in the plain" (and in one version: "among the oaks of Mamre the Amorite"). He was sitting at the door of his tent when the day grew hot. He lifted his eyes and looked, and behold, three men were standing over him. When he saw them, he hurried to them from the door of the tent (p-335) and bowed to the ground and said: "O Lord" (and in one version: "O friend of God"), "if I have found favor in Your sight, do not pass by your servant until I bring water to wash your feet. Rest under the tree and I will bring a little food, that you may refresh yourselves; after that you may pass on, since you have passed by your servant." They said to him: "Do as you have said." Abraham hurried and went into the tent to Sarah and said: "Quickly, take three measures of fine flour" (and in one version: "fine white flour"), "knead it and bake loaves from it." He ran to the herd of cattle, took a young, fat calf and gave it to the servant, and he ordered him to prepare it quickly. He also took curds and milk and the calf that had been prepared, and set it before them, while he himself stood before them under the tree. They said to him: "Where is Sarah your wife?" He said: "In the tent." He said: "I will return to you at this time next year, and Sarah will be alive and will have a son by you." Sarah heard it while she was at the door of the tent, hidden, and he was behind her. Abraham and Sarah were old and advanced in years, and the way of women had ceased for Sarah. So Sarah laughed inwardly and said: "After I have grown withered, shall I have pleasure, my lord being old?" The Lord said to Abraham: "Why did Sarah laugh, saying, 'Shall I really bear a child, now that I am old?' Is anything too hard for God? I will return to you at this time next year, and she will be alive and will have a son." Sarah denied it, saying: "I did not laugh," for she was frightened. He said: "No, but you did laugh." Then the men rose (p-336) and went toward Sodom and Amurah, and Abraham went with them to see them off. God said: "Shall I hide from Abraham My servant what I am doing? Abraham will become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth will be blessed by him, for I know that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord, to do righteousness and justice, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham all that He promised him." The Lord said [to Abraham]: "The outcry against Sodom and Amurah is great, and their sin is very grave." Then the men turned and went toward Sodom, while Abraham was still standing before the Lord. [Abraham drew near] and said: "O Lord, will You sweep away the righteous with the wicked? Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city; will You destroy it and not spare the place for the sake of the fifty righteous? Far be it from You, O Lord, to do such a thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous fare as the wicked! Far be it from You! Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?" The Lord said: "If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, I will spare the whole place for their sake." Abraham answered and said: "Behold, I have taken it upon myself to speak to the Lord, though I am but dust and ashes. Suppose the fifty righteous lack five; will You destroy the whole city for lack of five?" He said: "I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there." Abraham spoke to him again and said: "Suppose forty are found there?" He said: "I will not destroy it for the sake of forty." He said: "Let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak: suppose thirty are found there?" He said: "I will not do it if I find thirty there." He said: "Behold, I have taken it upon myself to speak to the Lord: suppose twenty are found there?" He said: "I will not destroy it for the sake of twenty." He said: "Let not the Lord be angry, and I will speak just this once: suppose ten are found there?" He said: "I will not destroy it for the sake of ten." So the Lord's appearing was withdrawn from Abraham when he had finished speaking, and Abraham returned to his place. (End.) The matter of Sarah's conception and giving birth has already passed in the Cow (sūrat al-Baqarah).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 77:

When the matter of giving them the good news to the friends (of God) and the destruction of the enemies had come to an end, and it was known from this that they did not descend except for momentous matters and wondrous circumstances, he began to relate their affair with Lut, peace be upon him, saying, conjoining it to what is implied: they did with Ibrahim the separation from Ibrahim, peace be upon him, of what has been mentioned, then they parted from him toward Lut, [and he did not mention the causal particle, because its context and the purpose of the surah do not require it, as we will indicate in al-'Ankabut]: ﴿And when Our messengers came﴾ in accordance with what Our greatness accompanied them with, ﴿to Lut﴾ after their separation from Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Between the two towns was eight miles, and it was said: four farsakh. They asked him to host them, and he had no choice (p-338) but to accept them, in keeping with what God enjoined regarding the guest, in conformity with the customs of the people of nobility. So he received them and resolved to defend them, seeing the goodliness of their forms and the splendour of their beauty, together with what he knew of the ugliness of his people's deeds and the wickedness of their inner natures. And when they came to him in this condition, ﴿he was grieved on their account﴾, that is: distress befell him because of their coming to his town, knowing the baseness of its people. Expressing this meaning in the passive voice is more vivid, more affecting to the soul, and more graceful. ﴿And he was straitened in regard to them﴾, that is: his dhar', meaning his capacity, that is its expansiveness in every [moment of] strength he was given. It is a proverb said of one who finds no way out from what is disliked. The root dh-r-‘ — in whatever order — revolves around expansiveness, because one measures out only what is abundant. Dhara'a al-raml: it spread out (sand). Mawt dhari': widespread death. Al-mudhar'a: one whose mother is Arab and whose father is not Arab, who is thus more widespread than one confined to one of the two. Al-dhari'a: that by which the hunter conceals himself, for it widens for him the hope that moves him to advance; and a ring on which archery is learned, because it accommodates the arrow, or because its hitter has wide mastery in the craft of archery. Al-wasila: because it conveys the one who seeks by it. Al-du'r: fear, because thought expands within it and admits even the slightest possibility. Al-'udhr: the widening of stratagem in a way that removes what appeared of shortcoming, from al-'adhawwar — for a wide-bellied donkey; it is also the king, for his breadth. Al-'idhar: the widest part of the face. A'dhartu al-ghulam: I circumcised the boy, i.e., you widened his foreskin (p-339). Al-i'dhar: food for circumcision and the like. ‘Udhrat al-jariya: the maiden's hymen, which necessitates her shrinking away out of fear for herself. Al-'udhra: a pain in the throat, which is its falling until one presses it; as if it was likened to the maiden's hymen in blocking the throat with what requires pressing. Likewise al-'udhra: for the forelock, because of exerting effort in defending it. Al-'adhra': a star which, when it rises, the heat intensifies and the surface of the earth spreads out. Al-'adhira (with fatha then kasra): the courtyard of the house, and by it the excrement was named. Al-'adhra': a piece of iron by which a person is tortured; it seems it was named so because it widens fear by precluding what would necessitate making an excuse, so that iron implement remains always virgin, with no one found to be tortured by it. As for 'adhdhara (with shadda), when it means to fall short, it is for negation: he did what has no excuse for it. Likewise ta'adhdhara al-amr: the matter became difficult, meaning that it avoided excuse, so no way remained for its ease. And a'dhara, when its faults multiply, i.e., he entered into what seeks an excuse for him, like anjada.

When He mentioned his condition, He mentioned his saying: ﴿And he said﴾, that is, Lut, ﴿This is a grievous day﴾, that is: extremely severe, because of my knowledge of the ignorance of those among whom I am. It is derived from 'asab, which is the tendons of the joints and their ligaments, and its core meaning revolves around severity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 78–80:

﴿And his people came hastening towards him﴾, that is, those who had the strength to attempt it. ﴿They were driven﴾, that is, as if something compelled them to that, which they could not resist, ﴿towards him﴾, that is, at the utmost haste, like one who is greedy and fearful of missing what he seeks, so he is agitated by it, or out of terror of Lut, peace be upon him, or of the angels, peace be upon them.

Since their finding [of the youths] and their disobedience ... did not extend over a period of time, he introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿And before this﴾, that is, before this coming, ﴿they used to﴾, that is, by natural disposition and inclination, ﴿do﴾, that is, continually, ﴿the evil deeds﴾, that is, the abominations whose evil is extreme, so they were accustomed to them and habituated to them until their sense of their ugliness disappeared. So he knew what they wanted. It seems they did not spare a handsome youth or any other stranger; therefore it is not mentioned that the messengers, peace be upon them, appeared in the form of handsome beardless youths, nor is the male in their story in any place restricted by beardlessness. It is as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" So it was said: ﴿He said: "O my people"﴾, appealing to them with gentleness, ﴿"these are my daughters"﴾, urging them towards modesty and generosity.

Since it was as if it were said, "What should we do with them?", he said: ﴿"They are purer for you"﴾. Since it was a situation of repelling with gentleness, he said, loosening the reins in granting that what they were doing was pure according to their claim, subtly pointing to the vileness of what they wanted: ﴿"They are purer for you"﴾. The intended meaning is not its literal sense, but rather alerting the people that they cannot reach them except by reaching his daughters, because the disgrace in both is equal, or in the guest it is greater. Similar to this is that a person intercedes for one who is about to be beaten; when the matter becomes grave, he throws himself upon him, so the image is that he did it to shield him from the beating with himself, and its meaning is honouring him by honouring him. On this is indicated His saying in the other verse: ﴿"If you are going to act"﴾ [al-Hijr: 71]. And here His saying: ﴿"So fear God"﴾, that is, the Greatest King in this matter that you intend, ﴿"and do not disgrace me"﴾, that is, do not bring upon me the scandal in which is humiliation, abasement and shame, ﴿"concerning my guests"﴾, for no one of sound mind doubts about this matter that if piety is present it prevents both of these matters, and that the disgrace, if piety is absent, is greater with regard to the daughters, because it is a shame that necessarily attaches to the father through the daughters.

All this is evidence that he did not doubt that they were human, and it did not occur to his mind that they were angels. So it is an alert to the disbelievers that no one benefits from the sending down of angels except the righteous, rightly-guided one who follows the truth. Then he denounced most strongly their state in that there would not be among them a rightly-guided man, urging them to desist from error and to adhere to the path of right guidance, so he said: ﴿"Is there not among you a man"﴾, that is, complete in manhood, ﴿"who is rightly-guided"﴾, complete in right guidance, to restrain you from this abomination. Evil (sū') is what its disagreeableness appears to its possessor; the grievous (ʿaṣīb) is the severe in evil specifically, as if its evil has wrapped around; strength (quwwah) specifically is that by which an act can occur or not occur; the pillar (rukn) is the support upon which a building rests after the foundation, and here the pillar is one who is like it; severity (shiddah) is a gathering in which possibility becomes difficult. The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 81:

When the opposition grew severe and the squeeze tightened, it was as if it were asked: "What did the messengers say to him?" It was said: ﴿They said﴾, and they signalled with the vocative particle (ḥarf al-nidā'), which is set for distance, to show that he had gone out of the house and bolted its door, and that the shouting was intense: ﴿O Lut﴾, indeed you take refuge in a strong pillar. Then they gave the reason for this by saying: ﴿Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you by your goodness and by all that you see of what distresses you and what gladdens you. Then, when this was established for him, it was certain that it was a cause for no harm coming near him in his company. So they made it clear by saying: ﴿They will not reach you﴾, without any need to link it with fa' (the conjunctive particle), meaning: and we are going to destroy them and overturn their cities upon them. ﴿So travel﴾, that is, go on by night, ﴿with your family﴾, making that journey and night-travel (al-isrā') a reality, ﴿in a portion﴾, that is, with a group, meaning while a part of the night still remains at your departure. ﴿And let none of you look back﴾, that is, do not look behind you and do not let anyone of your family turn back and lag behind, ﴿except your wife﴾. This is an exception from ﴿anyone﴾, in the nominative and accusative (raf' and naṣb), because a prohibited thing is like a negated thing in permitting both readings. The prohibition is addressed to him, peace be upon him, so the act is prohibited with respect to him, and negated with respect to them. It is possible that he took her out with him, because the meaning of the exception is that she was not commanded to travel by night with him, but she was forbidden from it; and her being excepted from the looking back with them indicates that there is no restriction on him in travelling with her. Or it means that she was behind them, so she followed them and looked back. Thus the reading in the accusative is from ﴿your family﴾, and the reading in the nominative is from ﴿anyone﴾. It does not follow from this that he commanded her to look back; rather, she differs from the one excepted in not being forbidden. For this reason they gave as the reason for what her being left out of the travel and the prohibition implies, that she would look back, by saying, emphasising it because the hope of her salvation is a strong mercy to her: ﴿Indeed, it [i.e., the matter] will befall her﴾, undoubtedly, ﴿what befalls them﴾, whether she looks back or not, whether she lags behind or not. Then it became clear to me from the expression, regarding her, with the active participle, and regarding them, with the past tense, that the punishment was decreed to befall them at this statement to Lut, peace be upon him, because their sins were complete. As for her, the decree concerning her is only finalised when her sins, on which the befalling is based, are complete, and that is at the looking back.

And when they expressed it in the past tense, to confirm that it would happen and to alert that her entering with them into the causes of the punishment had already occurred, this was a prompt to ask: has the striking of them drawn very near? It was said: Yes, and it was emphasised to confirm its occurrence, with delight in it, and because, given the nearness of the time, it would be denied: ﴿Indeed, their appointed time is the morning﴾, that is, the beginning of the seizing. It seems that Lut, peace be upon him, delayed with all his family and what would set them right, so his conduct was that of one who deems the morning far off. So they denied that by saying: ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾, that is, hasten to leave with those you have been commanded to take. And al-isrā' is travel by night, like al-surā.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 82–83:

When the admonishing and the advance warnings to Lot (peace be upon him) concerning what they were doing had ended, God, exalted is He, related the state of his people, saying: ﴿So when Our command came﴾. The particle *fa* (then) is used because of the causal and sequential linkage present in the story of Salih (peace be upon him). That is: when Lot left that place with his family, Our command came to us. When Our command came, which is Our punishment and the order to carry it out, ﴿We made﴾, by the majesty that belongs to Us, ﴿its highest part its lowest﴾, meaning the upper part of their cities became the lower part, while they were inside them (p. 346) ﴿and We rained upon it﴾, meaning upon their cities after overturning them on account of them. The reason the pronoun "hā" (its, feminine) is used here rather than "hum" (their) will be explained in surah al-Hijr. ﴿Stones of baked clay﴾, meaning sent down from a place of the utmost height, ﴿layered﴾, meaning the stones were piled one upon another within it, ﴿marked﴾, meaning marked with signs indicating that they were prepared for punishment. From *al-simah* (mark), and *al-sawmah* is the mark placed on grazing camels so that they can be distinguished when they mix in the pasture. In surah al-Dhariyat it says: ﴿stones of clay﴾ (Dhariyat 51:33). This is because the origin of stones is earth, into which God places, through water, the capacity to become stone, just as He placed in it the capacity to be transformed into ores such as gold, silver, iron and others. Thus, with respect to its origin it is clay, and with respect to its first stage it is stone, sulphur and fire. Perhaps sulphur-stone is the heaviest of stones, together with the strength of fire and the foulness of its smell. Then He magnified them by saying: ﴿with your Lord﴾, and He used the term "Lord" to indicate the abundance of His kindness and His bounty, and that He ordered him (ﷺ) to warn only out of mercy to his community, which He made the best of nations and will make the most numerous of nations, and He will not destroy them as He destroyed those people.

The root *s-j-l*, in whatever order its letters are arranged, revolves around height: from *al-jals* (a raised ground) as opposed to a low valley, which is *al-najd* (high land), and it entails thickness and height. From thickness comes *al-jals* for thick ground and a strong camel. Height entails rectification (*al-taswib*). From *jalasa*, meaning he sat down. *Al-sajl* is a large bucket, and it usually works in pairs, so that when one descends the other rises; hence *al-musajalah* means rivalry and boasting. *Al-sajl* also means a large udder. *Al-sijill* (with a kasra and a doubled lam) means a book, because in it is recorded what brings boasting and contention. *Salaja al-ta'am* means he swallowed the food. *Al-sullajan* is a soft plant, as if it was so named because its branches bend downward because of their softness. This meaning has been indicated in this verse by three things: the raining down, the word "upon" (*ala*), and *sijjil*.

Since the meaning is that they came from a place of the utmost height, so that their impact would be greater, it is most fitting to follow this with His saying: ﴿and they are not﴾, despite the severity [of the punishment] after its place (of origin), ﴿far from the wrongdoers﴾, meaning from any one of the two groups most deeply involved in wrongdoing at that time, nor from this (group) nor from any other time period, ﴿far﴾, so that it is not supposed that reaching them with it required a long time.

The mention of this story in the Torah: In the first book, after what has passed concerning the glad tidings given to Abraham (peace be upon him), it says: "The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting at the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them he went to meet them, and bowed with his face to the ground, and said: 'I beg you, my lords, turn aside to your servant's house, spend the night there, wash your feet, rise early and go on your way.' They said: 'No, we will spend the night in the street.' But Lot urged them strongly, so they turned aside with him and entered his house. He prepared a meal for them, and before they lay down to sleep, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, young and old, all the people together, (p. 348) and they called Lot and said to him: 'Where are the two men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us that we may know them.' (In another copy: 'that we may lie with them.') So Lot went out to them and shut the door behind him, and said to them: 'Do not do wrong to me, my brothers! Here, I have two daughters who have not known a man; let me bring them out to you, and do to them whatever seems good in your eyes, but do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof.' They said to him: 'Stand aside! This one came to live among us and now acts as our judge. Now we will treat you worse than them.' Lot pressed the people hard, and they came near to break down the door, but the two men stretched out their hands, drew Lot into the house with them, and shut the door. Then they struck the men who were at the door, small and great, with blindness, so that they were weary trying to find the door. The two angels said to Lot: 'What are you doing here? Take your sons-in-law, your sons and your daughters, and everything you have in this city, and bring them out of this place, for we are going to destroy this city, because their outcry and the wickedness of their deeds has reached the Lord; the Lord has sent us to destroy it.' So Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, the husbands of his daughters, and said: 'Get up, leave this city, for the Lord is about to destroy it.' But he seemed to his sons-in-law like one who was joking. When morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying: 'Get up, take your wife and your two daughters who are here with you, lest you be swept away in the sins of this city.' But Lot hesitated, so the two angels took him by the hand, and his wife, and his two daughters, because the Lord had mercy on him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city. When they had brought them out (p. 349), they said: 'Escape for your life; do not look back, and do not stop anywhere in the whole plain; flee to the mountain, lest you be swept away.' Lot said to them: 'I beg you, my lords, let me find favour in your sight now, for your servant has received great mercy and kindness from you, which you have shown to me in saving my life. I cannot escape to the mountain, lest the evil overtake me and I die. This city is near enough to flee to, and it is small. Please let me flee there, for it is small; let my life be spared.' He said to him: 'I have granted you this request also; I will not overthrow this city of which you speak. Hurry, escape there, for we cannot do anything until you have entered it.' Therefore the city was called Zoar (in another copy: Zughar). The sun had risen upon the earth when Lot entered Zoar (in another copy: Zughar). Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven, and He overthrew those cities and the whole plain, and destroyed all the inhabitants of the cities and all that lived there and all the vegetation of the land. But his wife looked back behind her, and she became a pillar of salt. Abraham rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before the Lord; he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the plain, and he saw that the smoke of the land rose like the smoke of a furnace. When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the overturning, when He overthrew the cities in which Lot had dwelt. So Lot went up from Zoar (in another copy: Zughar) (p. 350) and dwelt in the mountain with his two daughters, for he feared to dwell in Zoar; so he lived in a cave."
