The particle *fa* (then) is used because of the causal and sequential linkage present in the story of Salih (peace be upon him). That is: when Lot left that place with his family, Our command came to us. When Our command came, which is Our punishment and the order to carry it out, ﴿We made﴾, by the majesty that belongs to Us, ﴿its highest part its lowest﴾, meaning the upper part of their cities became the lower part, while they were inside them (p. 346) ﴿and We rained upon it﴾, meaning upon their cities after overturning them on account of them. The reason the pronoun "hā" (its, feminine) is used here rather than "hum" (their) will be explained in surah al-Hijr. ﴿Stones of baked clay﴾, meaning sent down from a place of the utmost height, ﴿layered﴾, meaning the stones were piled one upon another within it, ﴿marked﴾, meaning marked with signs indicating that they were prepared for punishment. From *al-simah* (mark), and *al-sawmah* is the mark placed on grazing camels so that they can be distinguished when they mix in the pasture. In surah al-Dhariyat it says: ﴿stones of clay﴾ (Dhariyat 51:33). This is because the origin of stones is earth, into which God places, through water, the capacity to become stone, just as He placed in it the capacity to be transformed into ores such as gold, silver, iron and others. Thus, with respect to its origin it is clay, and with respect to its first stage it is stone, sulphur and fire. Perhaps sulphur-stone is the heaviest of stones, together with the strength of fire and the foulness of its smell. Then He magnified them by saying: ﴿with your Lord﴾, and He used the term "Lord" to indicate the abundance of His kindness and His bounty, and that He ordered him (ﷺ) to warn only out of mercy to his community, which He made the best of nations and will make the most numerous of nations, and He will not destroy them as He destroyed those people.

The root *s-j-l*, in whatever order its letters are arranged, revolves around height: from *al-jals* (a raised ground) as opposed to a low valley, which is *al-najd* (high land), and it entails thickness and height. From thickness comes *al-jals* for thick ground and a strong camel. Height entails rectification (*al-taswib*). From *jalasa*, meaning he sat down. *Al-sajl* is a large bucket, and it usually works in pairs, so that when one descends the other rises; hence *al-musajalah* means rivalry and boasting. *Al-sajl* also means a large udder. *Al-sijill* (with a kasra and a doubled lam) means a book, because in it is recorded what brings boasting and contention. *Salaja al-ta'am* means he swallowed the food. *Al-sullajan* is a soft plant, as if it was so named because its branches bend downward because of their softness. This meaning has been indicated in this verse by three things: the raining down, the word "upon" (*ala*), and *sijjil*.

Since the meaning is that they came from a place of the utmost height, so that their impact would be greater, it is most fitting to follow this with His saying: ﴿and they are not﴾, despite the severity [of the punishment] after its place (of origin), ﴿far from the wrongdoers﴾, meaning from any one of the two groups most deeply involved in wrongdoing at that time, nor from this (group) nor from any other time period, ﴿far﴾, so that it is not supposed that reaching them with it required a long time.

The mention of this story in the Torah: In the first book, after what has passed concerning the glad tidings given to Abraham (peace be upon him), it says: "The two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting at the gate of Sodom. When Lot saw them he went to meet them, and bowed with his face to the ground, and said: 'I beg you, my lords, turn aside to your servant's house, spend the night there, wash your feet, rise early and go on your way.' They said: 'No, we will spend the night in the street.' But Lot urged them strongly, so they turned aside with him and entered his house. He prepared a meal for them, and before they lay down to sleep, the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, young and old, all the people together, (p. 348) and they called Lot and said to him: 'Where are the two men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us that we may know them.' (In another copy: 'that we may lie with them.') So Lot went out to them and shut the door behind him, and said to them: 'Do not do wrong to me, my brothers! Here, I have two daughters who have not known a man; let me bring them out to you, and do to them whatever seems good in your eyes, but do nothing to these men, for they have come under the shelter of my roof.' They said to him: 'Stand aside! This one came to live among us and now acts as our judge. Now we will treat you worse than them.' Lot pressed the people hard, and they came near to break down the door, but the two men stretched out their hands, drew Lot into the house with them, and shut the door. Then they struck the men who were at the door, small and great, with blindness, so that they were weary trying to find the door. The two angels said to Lot: 'What are you doing here? Take your sons-in-law, your sons and your daughters, and everything you have in this city, and bring them out of this place, for we are going to destroy this city, because their outcry and the wickedness of their deeds has reached the Lord; the Lord has sent us to destroy it.' So Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law, the husbands of his daughters, and said: 'Get up, leave this city, for the Lord is about to destroy it.' But he seemed to his sons-in-law like one who was joking. When morning dawned, the angels urged Lot, saying: 'Get up, take your wife and your two daughters who are here with you, lest you be swept away in the sins of this city.' But Lot hesitated, so the two angels took him by the hand, and his wife, and his two daughters, because the Lord had mercy on him, and they brought him out and set him outside the city. When they had brought them out (p. 349), they said: 'Escape for your life; do not look back, and do not stop anywhere in the whole plain; flee to the mountain, lest you be swept away.' Lot said to them: 'I beg you, my lords, let me find favour in your sight now, for your servant has received great mercy and kindness from you, which you have shown to me in saving my life. I cannot escape to the mountain, lest the evil overtake me and I die. This city is near enough to flee to, and it is small. Please let me flee there, for it is small; let my life be spared.' He said to him: 'I have granted you this request also; I will not overthrow this city of which you speak. Hurry, escape there, for we cannot do anything until you have entered it.' Therefore the city was called Zoar (in another copy: Zughar). The sun had risen upon the earth when Lot entered Zoar (in another copy: Zughar). Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven, and He overthrew those cities and the whole plain, and destroyed all the inhabitants of the cities and all that lived there and all the vegetation of the land. But his wife looked back behind her, and she became a pillar of salt. Abraham rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before the Lord; he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of the plain, and he saw that the smoke of the land rose like the smoke of a furnace. When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the overturning, when He overthrew the cities in which Lot had dwelt. So Lot went up from Zoar (in another copy: Zughar) (p. 350) and dwelt in the mountain with his two daughters, for he feared to dwell in Zoar; so he lived in a cave."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 84:

When the story, which informs of what Lut, peace be upon him, undertook of God's command without slackening, neither out of desire nor out of fear, and of the peril involved in the descent of the angels, had come to an end, it was followed by the closest of the famous stories to it in time. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to﴾, meaning: We certainly sent to ﴿Madyan﴾, who were the tribe of their forefather Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, ﴿their brother Shu'ayb﴾. So it is as if someone said: What did he say to them? It was said: ﴿He said﴾ what his brothers among the prophets said at the outset concerning the root of religion: ﴿O my people﴾, seeking their sympathy and showing the utmost compassion, ﴿worship God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, not associating anything with Him, for He is One, ﴿you have no﴾, and he went to the extreme in negation, saying: ﴿deity other than Him﴾. So their words, as you see, agreed and their call was united to God alone. This alone is decisive in its indication of the truthfulness of each of them, since it is known with certainty that their eras were far apart and their dwellings distant, and that none of them had studied the sciences or known the news of people except from the Living, the Self-Subsisting.

Imam Shihab al-Din Umar ibn Muhammad al-Suhrawardi said in his book "Rashf al-Nasa'ih al-Imaniyya wa Kashf al-Fada'ih al-Yunaniyya" in mention of the prophets: Their sources were united, as if they were a solid structure. They expressed themselves in different tongues that lead to one connected sea, joined to the hearts and one with them, drawing from the ocean that encompasses the worlds of witnessing and the unseen. The sources of the laws differed according to what divine wisdom required for the benefit of the people of each age and each religious community. Their disagreement in the subsidiary matters did not harm them, given their unity in the fundamentals. He said before this: When the philosophers did not draw from the seas of the prophets, the steeds of their thoughts halted with them in the world of witnessing. When they attempted to plunge into divine matters, the nakedness of their ignorance was exposed, and they were disgraced by their confusion and disagreement: ﴿You would think them united, but their hearts are divided﴾ [al-Hashr: 14]. The course of thought was cut off for them at the limit of the world of dominion and witnessing, and Alexander did not enter their view into the darkness of the world of the unseen until they might obtain the Fountain of Life, whoever drinks from which does not die. End of quote.

When he called them to justice between themselves and God, he called them to justice between themselves and His servants, regarding the most reprehensible of what they had adopted as a habit after shirk. So he said: ﴿And do not diminish﴾, meaning: in any way whatsoever, ﴿the measure and the scale﴾, neither the measuring nor its instrument, nor the weighing nor its instrument. Measuring (kayl) is the equalizing of a thing by an instrument in terms of quantity, and weighing (wazn) is its equalizing in terms of lightness and heaviness. Thus measuring is for justice in quantity, and weighing is for justice in quality. Then he gave the reason for that by his saying: ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity﴾, meaning: in abundance that makes you independent of defrauding, warning and encouraging at once, with an indication that disbelief necessitates retribution just as gratitude necessitates blessing.

Since it was as if it were said: "Indeed, I fear for you poverty through diminishing," he followed it, emphasizing their denial: ﴿And indeed, I fear for you﴾ because of it and because of shirk ﴿the punishment of an encompassing day﴾, encompassing you in the small and the great, and your wealth, the good and the bad, meaning: destroying, like His saying: ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Its origin is from the encompassing of an enemy. Describing the day as encompassing is more eloquent, because it encompasses what is in it of punishment and other things, and punishment encompasses the one punished; so mentioning the encompassing [by the encompassing] is more terrifying. It is what surrounds a thing from every side, and that occurs by the meeting of its two ends. Diminishing is taking some of a quantity, just as increasing is adding something to it, and both are a departure from the measure. Weighing is equalizing a thing by the balance, just as measuring is equalizing it by the measure. From the encompassing is what Ibn Majah narrated from Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "No people diminished the measure and the scale except that they were seized with years of drought, hardship of livelihood, and the tyranny of the ruler over them. And they did not withhold the zakat of their wealth except that they were denied rain from the sky, and were it not for the animals, they would not have been given rain."

[p. 353]

Since the absence of deficiency might be taken to imply mere approximation, he followed it with what negates this possibility. This also alerts that it is not enough merely to refrain from deliberately cheating in measure, but that striving to give full measure is required, even with an excess that cannot be achieved without it. Moreover, explicitly commanding a thing after forbidding its opposite is more emphatic. So he said, appealing to them with a reminder that he is one of them, so that what grieves them grieves him, and that because God has given them strength, they are worthy of turning away from pursuing base morals and their vices:

﴿And O my people﴾, i.e., O you who have strength in standing up to what befalls you, ﴿give full measure and weight﴾, i.e., complete it in a good manner, ﴿the measure and the scale﴾ [i.e., the measured goods and the weighed goods and their instruments]. He emphasized this with His saying ﴿with justice﴾, i.e., with upright equity. Thus fulfilment is commanded in these two sentences repeatedly, as emphasis for it, eagerness for it, and a manifestation of the universality of its benefit and the comprehensiveness of its blessing. By the whole, the suspicion of *majaz* (figurative usage) is removed in the most eloquent way. It has already passed in al-An'am, and it will come in this surah at ﴿not diminished﴾ [Hud: 109], that a thing may be used figuratively for what approximates it. Then he further emphasized it by generalizing the prohibition against every deficiency, by this and other means, in all wealth, so he said: ﴿And do not diminish﴾, i.e., do not reduce [in a manner of denial and humiliation] ﴿people's things﴾. Then he showed that their actions are the fruit of rushing in without thought, since they do not arise from any law. Their first is foolishness and their last is corruption. So he said: ﴿And do not act wickedly in the earth﴾, i.e., do not conduct yourselves and move about in it without insight or reflection, while you are ﴿causing corruption﴾, i.e., doing what is corruption in meaning just as it is corruption in form. Thus it is a call to prioritizing reflection and deliberation before every act. This is because the root *'athā* (عثى), in every arrangement, revolves around seeking without insight, from *al-'ayth* (العيث), for easy land, for its ease people are deceived by it, and the ignorant one treads it without guidance, so ignorance and confusion result. From it comes *al-ta'yīth* (التعييث), for the blind man's seeking of a thing. *Al-a'thā* is the stupid, heavy one, and the color inclining to black, and the very hairy one. This entails following desire, so corruption and hastening in it result, and that is the meaning of *al-'uthiyy* (العثي). The linguists said: *'athā* and *'āthā* mean: he corrupted. In al-Zubaydi's *Mukhtasar al-'Ayn*: *'athā* in the earth means *'āthā yaʿīthu ʿaythan*, which is hastening in corruption. So the meaning, according to the majority, is: do not commit corruption deliberately, which is clear; according to what I have estimated of the original meaning, which is for the revolving-point, it is clearer; and according to what al-Zubaydi said: do not hasten in it. It should not be supposed that hastening is then a condition, such that the prohibition would be directed at it. Rather, it is an indication that advancing without reflection happens only in this way, since it accords with desire. And God knows best. *Al-wafā'* is the completion of the right; *al-bakhs* is deficiency. So it is more specific than injustice, because it is placing a thing in other than its proper place.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 86:

Since their concern after shirk was confined to wealth, and his forbidding them what he forbade them was, in their assumption, bound to diminish it, they were as if they had said: "If we follow you in what you say, our wealth will perish or dwindle, and our circumstances will be reduced to ruin, so nothing will remain for us?" He said: ﴿What remains with Allah﴾, that is: the bounty of the Sovereign Most High, who combines all the attributes of perfection, and His blessing in your wealth and in all your circumstances, and His preserving for you His regard, which necessitates His pardon, which is the fruit of following His command, ﴿is better for you﴾ than what you suppose to be an increase through deficiency and wrongdoing. This is because the remainder (baqiyyah) of a thing is what is left over from it. It may also carry the sense of buqya (preservation), from abqa 'alayhi, yubqi, ibqa' (he spared him), and istabqaytu fulanan (I kept someone alive), when you pardon his sin, as if that sin had made his affection perish or had caused it to perish in your sight; so when you spare him, you have abandoned what had been due. They also say: "I see you keeping this with your sight," meaning when one keeps looking at it. This was stated by Imam Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qazzaz in his comprehensive Diwan, and the explanation of what this root revolves around will come at the end of the surah.

Since the goodness of what justice leaves behind is manifest in a place that is not hidden from any person of understanding, He left it aside and clarified its condition in His saying: ﴿if you are﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, ﴿believers﴾, that is, firmly established in faith, indicating that its goodness for one who is not a believer rests on no foundation, so it is of no benefit except in this world, and it is therefore nothing, due to the swiftness of its passing, departure from it, and removal. The conjunction "wa" (and) indicates an unmentioned element, meaning: "So believe, acting upon what I have commanded you, so that you may attain the good." ﴿For I am only a warner﴾ ﴿and I am not﴾, and he placed first what they might imagine of his intent, to deny it with emphasis, saying: ﴿over you﴾, and he went to the extreme in negation, saying: ﴿a guardian﴾, one who knows all your deeds [and your circumstances] and has power to restrain you from whatever of them would be corruption. The root of baqiyyah is leaving something of a thing that has already passed.

(p. 356) Since the upshot of what Shu'ayb called them to was abandoning what their forefathers were upon of foolishness, both toward the Creator, through associating partners with Him, and toward creatures, through treachery, and since that abandonment was in their view severance and folly, it became a touchstone for minds and a cutting edge for opinions, by which the keen is distinguished from the dull. It was as if it were said: "What did they say?" So it was said: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb!"﴾ They called him by his name, out of coarseness and harshness, and they denied it to him, mocking his prayer: ﴿Does your prayer command you﴾, meaning: does it make you act as one who constantly commands us to perform obligations, ﴿that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we stop doing﴾, meaning: habitually, ﴿with our property what we wish﴾, such as clipping dirhams and dinars, corrupting transactions, gambling, and the like, of what constitutes the corruption of wealth. They mean that what you command us does not proceed along the path of reason. So what commands you is nothing but what we see you doing of this thing you call prayer; that is, it belongs to the category of your act of prayer.

The root ṣ-l-w (ṣ-l-w) is both waw-final and ya-final, both hamzated and unhamzated, in all its permutations, and it revolves around the notion of connection (waṣlah). Thus ṣalāh (prayer) is for the servant's connection with his Lord, and likewise supplication (du'ā') and seeking forgiveness (istighfār). The ṣalawāt of the Jews are their churches, in which they gather. The ṣalā is the middle of the back and its gathering place, and also what surrounds the tail. Al-muṣalli among horses is the one that follows the leader. Ṣāla al-faḥl means the stallion charged upon the herd of wild asses. Ṣalā al-rajulu, and ṣalaya, means he defamed him, as if you had attached the fault to him. The notion of connection is clear in this, and it seems to be the reality from which all the meanings of the root branched out. Its explanation will come at the words of the Exalted, ﴿in the mornings and evenings﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15], in Surat al-Ra'd, God willing.

The meaning of the verse then is: Does what you undergo of prayers, the actual ones with their pillars and the spiritual ones of supplication, seeking forgiveness, and all acts of righteousness that carry one to kinds of connection and forbid every severance, command you to openly sever ourselves from our fathers, while supposing that they are present and witnessing what we do that opposes their aims, and to abandon the increase of our wealth, which is loss? Together with contravening the deeds of the fathers, this is extravagance, and so it is folly. Their doubt on both matters revolved around imitating the fathers and holding them free from error, on the possibility that their deeds had some aspect of correctness hidden from them. They also added, regarding wealth, the assumption of extravagance. Thus by calling us to each of these two matters, you have become, in that case, one who calls to the opposite of what you yourself are engaged in. ﴿Indeed you﴾, then, ﴿are the only﴾ ﴿forbearing﴾ in your acceptance of what angers those of kinship, ﴿the rightly guided﴾ in squandering wealth. By this, as they claimed, they intended to strip him of every quality he possesses beyond them, of these two surpassing attributes, with what their foolishness imagined to be a decisive proof against him. By this they meant attributing to him folly and error, in the manner of mockery.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 88:

When they accused him of severing ties and of foolishness, he began to refute what they had said and to deny the accusation contained in it. It was presented in the form of an answer, as if someone had said: "What did he answer them with?" So it was said: (p-358) ﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, who has bestowed upon me what is a kindness to you as well,"﴾ appealing to them by the bonds of kinship that exist between them, and alerting them to the goodness of reflecting on what he has put forward as a supposition and hypothesis, so that it might be more conducive to agreement and fairness. ﴿Tell me﴾, that is: inform me. ﴿If I am﴾, that is: in a state that is at the utmost firmness, ﴿upon a clear proof﴾, that is: an evidence, ﴿from my Lord﴾, who has shown me a kindness that is also a kindness to you. He joined to the conditional clause whose meaning is being asked about his statement: "and" he has "provided me" [with sustenance], and he magnified the provision by saying: ﴿from Him a good provision﴾, that is: a noble provision and abundant lawful wealth, in which I have wronged no one. The answer is omitted so that the soul may go off in every direction. It is possible to say in this regard: Would it befit a reasonable person to attribute to me foolishness in squandering wealth by abandoning wrongdoing, or would it befit me to be forbearing toward one who worships other than Him and to abandon calling you to God? Thus it has become clear by this that I have not commanded you to what displeases you, namely abandoning what you are accustomed to, and I have not exposed myself to the anger of all of you, and I have not left the likes of your deeds except out of fear of His anger and hope for His pleasure. It is therefore manifest that there is no accusation or error in any matter of mine: I have never done what I forbade you from in the past. ﴿And I do not wish﴾, that is: at any time, ﴿to oppose you﴾, that is: [by] going off alone ﴿to what I forbid you from﴾ in the future. My wealth has not diminished by abandoning the likes of your deeds. This is guidance toward reflection on the matter of:

*Do not forbid a trait while committing its like; it is a disgrace upon you when you do it, and great.*

*Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error; when you have desisted from it, then you are wise.*

(p-359) [These three answers have alerted to the fact that the reasonable person must observe, in everything he does and forsakes, one of three rights: the most important and highest of them is the right of God; the second is the right of the self; and the third is the right of the servants, all in sincerity.] Thus it was established, through his distance from accusation together with the soundness of his actions and the goodness of his intentions, that his forbearance ﷺ and his rectitude were manifest. Therefore he followed it with what contains its meaning, stated explicitly, saying: ﴿I do not wish﴾, that is: [I wish] for nothing among things, ﴿except reform﴾, and he acknowledged his inability, saying: ﴿as much as I am able﴾, that is: for the duration of my ability to do good, and this is as I intended, for my wealth, together with my avoidance of what you are upon, is good and is not less than the wealth of any one of you. Thus it is known by observation that there is no squandering in justice. As for monotheism, it is, together with the absence of accusation against me in it, a call to the One Who is capable of everything, besides Whom there is no good and from Whom there is no escape except by returning to Him. Then he disavowed power and strength and ascribed the matter to the One to whom it belongs, saying: ﴿And my success is not but through God﴾, that is: in what I am able to do of reforming action, ﴿but through God﴾, that is: the One to whom all perfection belongs. Then he made clear that He is the one worthy of being hoped in, saying, pointing to pure monotheism, which is the highest rank of knowledge of the Origin: ﴿Upon Him﴾, that is: alone, ﴿I have relied﴾. Since he sought from God success in attaining the truth in what he does and forsakes, and seeking help from Him in the totality of his affairs, and turned to Him with his whole being, and cut off the hopes of the disbelievers from him, and manifested his freedom from them and his indifference to them, and since in his saying: ﴿as much as I am able﴾ (p-360) there was an acknowledgment that he is the locus of shortcoming, he informed them that he continually renews repentance because of the greatness of the matter. He expressed this with a phrase suitable for warning against the Day of Resurrection, as a threat to them, saying, alerting to the knowledge of the Return so that faith in God and the Last Day would be complete: ﴿And to Him alone I turn back﴾, that is: I return; in meaning, [it refers to] my precedence in repentance, and in sensory terms, my certainty of resurrection after death. Success (tawfiq) is the creation of the power for what is in accordance with the command, of obedience, from conformity to correspondence. Reliance upon God (tawakkul) is the committing of the matter to Him with contentment in His management, together with holding fast to His obedience.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 89:

When he had shown them his excuse, by which the accusation against him was removed, he followed it with what shows them that the truth had become so clear to them that nothing remained with it except obstinate opposition. So he warned them of its consequences and reminded them of the case of those who committed it, saying: ﴿O my people﴾, and the people most dear to me, ﴿let not my defiance (shiqaq) of you lead you﴾, i.e., let not your defiance of me lead you, ﴿to suffer﴾ from the punishment ﴿the like of what befell the people of Noah﴾ [i.e., the punishment that] ﴿befell the people of Noah﴾ after the length of their lifespans and the remoteness of their lands, ﴿or the people of Hud﴾ despite the strength of their bodies and the persistence of their security, ﴿or the people of Salih﴾ despite their hewing of houses out of the rocks and their raising of lofty palaces.

When the nearness (of the two peoples) produced the effect of similarity in form (mushakala) and fitting relation (munasaba), he changed the style to magnify the terror, saying: ﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ [i.e.] in the wickedness of their deeds, the evil of their condition, the severity of their punishment and their retribution. ﴿Are not far from you﴾ [i.e.] neither in time nor in place. You are therefore the most fitting of people to remember their condition, so that you may take warning from it. I interpreted "jarama" as "hamala" (to bear, to carry someone to), because Ibn al-Qattaa' reported that it is said: "jaramtu al-rajul" (I made the man), meaning: "hamaltuhu 'ala al-shay'" (I drove him to the thing). Al-Rummani attributed this interpretation to al-Hasan and Qatada. It is also permissible to interpret it according to what the root (madda) revolves around, namely cutting (qat'), i.e., let not my defiance of you cut you off from following what I call you to, out of fear that it will befall you. Al-Rummani also permitted this.

When he had warned them, he followed it with encouragement, in a context indicating that if they did not hasten to repentance, punishment would overtake them. He said, linking this command to that prior prohibition: ﴿And ask your Lord for forgiveness﴾, i.e., seek the concealment of the One who has been good to you. He indicated the measure of repentance by the particle of delay, saying: ﴿Then turn to Him in repentance﴾. Then he gave a reason for this, encouraging them to turn toward Him, by saying: ﴿Indeed, my Lord﴾, i.e., the One who is singularly mine, with the good you see in terms of religion and worldly life, ﴿is Merciful and Loving﴾, i.e., abundant in honoring those who return to Him, by preserving them in what He is pleased with, and abundant in showing affection toward him. He did not begin with the address of entreaty as was his custom, by saying: "O my people," indicating that there was no longer time left for me in which I could feel secure from the descent of punishment so that I could occupy myself in it with entreaty. Perhaps the matter is more hasty than that, so seek His forgiveness by making it your aim, then reach it through repentance. Thus "thumma" (then) is on its proper track of sequence, and as for the delay, it is in consideration of the great measure of repentance and its elevated rank, (p-362) because forgiveness is not obtained through seeking unless it is accompanied by repentance. This is the case with every grave sin: it is not expiated except by repentance. That is because the obedience performed after it becomes, in kind, equal to it as a great matter among acts of obedience, [just as that sin is a great matter in the kind of disobediences, so obedience does not have the power to erase it, and the repetition] of acts of obedience is countered by the repetition of disobedience through persistence, which is in the position of repeating the act of disobedience in every state.

When they saw that he would not desist from them, and could not answer his speech, they despaired him of returning to them. They did so by lowering themselves, out of obstinacy in understanding this very clear speech, to the rank of beasts, and they threatened him. So Allah the Exalted informed about them [of that] as a resumption (isti'naf), answering one who asks: what did they say after this good supplication? By His words: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb"﴾, calling him by his name in rudeness and harshness, ﴿"We do not understand much of what you say"﴾. That is, now, because "ma" (what) specifies the present state. And if much of the speech is not understood, its intended meaning is not understood. They mean: calm yourself and leave off your speech, for we do not understand it, treating him with contempt, just as a person says to his opponent when he accuses him of raving: "I do not know what you are saying." Since their aim, along with their obstinacy, was to end the matter, they restricted the lack of understanding to "much" so that it would be closer to possibility. And it seems that they, and Allah knows best, were indicating that it is speech without coherence, so it has no import and its content has no existence in reality.

Since this implied that he was weak of intellect, because his speech was like the speech of madmen (p-٣٦٣), they followed it with their saying: ﴿"And indeed we see you among us as weak"﴾, that is, a repeated and continuous seeing, ﴿weak﴾ in body and otherwise. So do not expose yourself to our wrath, for you cannot avoid any harm we inflict upon you, by strength of intellect, body, or kinsmen. They also indicated the weakness of his kinsmen by their expression "a group" (rahṭ) in their saying: ﴿"And were it not for your group, we would have stoned you"﴾, that is, we would have killed you in the worst manner. The rahṭ is from three to ten, and it has been said most commonly that his clan numbered forty. So you are not one who can prevail over us, given your weakness and the small number of your people. ﴿"And you are not"﴾, that is, by yourself, since "ma" for negating the present state implies restriction to time, and the rule is that what follows it should be a verb or its equivalent. Since it is followed by a noun, especially a pronoun, this indicates that the fronting is for emphasis and restriction. ﴿"Over us, a mighty one"﴾, that is, a dear one loved by us. You say "a'azztu fulānan" (I held someone dear) when he has affection for you. Rather, your people are the dear ones to us, because they agree with us. If the intended meaning were "you are not dear to us," the answer would be: "why would I not be dear, when Allah has honored me?" or something similar. It is also possible that "mighty" (ʿazīz) means strong and unassailable, and their understanding of their group's immunity would then be taken to mean that what restrains them is their agreement with them, not their strength. And "fiqh" (understanding) (fiqh) means comprehending speech according to what it contains of meaning, and it has become the name of a branch of the religious sciences. The root of "rahṭ" is strength, from "tarhīṭ" for the intensity of eating; from it comes "al-rāhiṭāʾ," the burrow of the jerboa, for its strength and solidity, so that its young may hide in it.

When Their singling out of the denial of might to him (Shu'ayb) implies that his kinsmen are mighty in their eyes, he rebuked them for this in a context of warning them. So Allah, the Exalted, said, relating from him as a resumption: ﴿He said﴾ (p-364), that is, Shu'ayb, ﴿"O my people,﴾ and the matter did not lack an appeal and an entreaty through mention of the tender bond of kinship, ﴿"Is my clan﴾ that is, my nearest relatives among you, ﴿more esteemed by you than Allah?"﴾ That is, the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, so that you looked to them on my account because of my kinship with them, and you did not look to Allah on account of my nearness to Him, by the honour from Him that became manifest upon me. ﴿And you have put Him﴾ that is, by what you have imposed upon yourselves, which is contrary to the primordial natural disposition (fitrah), ﴿behind your backs.﴾ That is, you turned away from Him with the aversion of one who places a thing behind him. He clarified the meaning of "behind" by His saying: ﴿"Cast away"﴾ that is, you have made Him like a thing absent from you, forgotten by you, one that is not regarded, and you did not keep Him in mind regarding me, given my attribution to Him through prophethood and servanthood.

Since the meaning of the speech, for the sake of rebuke, is: you have reversed things in action, so you did not recognise the truth for its people, for it was fitting for you not to forget Allah but to keep Him in mind in all your affairs, the explanation of this understanding was apt with His saying: ﴿"Indeed, my Lord﴾ that is, the One who is good to me. And since the intent was to emphasise the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, the Exalted, of their deeds, He placed before it His saying: ﴿"is Encompassing of what you do"﴾ of the great and the small. So He is capable over every act of yours, to carry it out or to nullify it. Thus He encompasses you; He does not turn back from my support against you, nor from bringing you down, out of regard for anyone of might or power. Rather, you have with Him a term, by which He will delay you, for He does not fear escape. And "ittikhadh" (taking) is the taking of a thing for a matter that continues in what follows, like the taking of a house. And "muhit" (encompassing) is one who governs a thing like a wall that encloses it, such that (p-365) nothing of it escapes him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 93:

When He concluded the verse with their threat by what He made clear, that their threat to him is worthless and he does not care about it, He followed it with what confirms it, namely that he is not abandoning any of his work, of that to which they have been disposed, and He increased the threat, saying: ﴿And O my people, act according to your position﴾, meaning: carry out the work for whatever you wish, firm and dominant, ﴿upon your standing﴾, meaning: your state by which you are able to carry out work. ﴿Indeed, I am acting﴾ upon what has become my standing, meaning a state by which I am able to carry out work, from which I never cease: my warning to those who disbelieve, my giving good news to those who believe, and my carrying out everything that the King has obligated upon me, not fearing you, not dreading you, not hoping for your companionship, and not relying on anyone other than Him.

Since their persistence in their deeds was a cause for the occurrence of the punishment they were threatened with, and its occurrence was a cause for knowing who will be disgraced, He mentioned it after this threat, so the omission of the fa' in His saying ﴿You will know﴾ is good. Meaning: with a promise that does not fail, even if its time is delayed, and its being placed in the manner of an answer for one who seems to say: What is meant by this command to work, which was emphasized as a prohibition before? What clarifies it has already preceded in the story of Noah, peace be upon him. And better than this: when they said ﴿We do not understand much of what you say﴾ [Hud: 91], their lying, in presenting the speech as if answering the question of one whose entire thought is directed to his speech, is a speaker saying: What will happen if we act and you act? This is a hidden connection indicating the presumed question; had He mentioned the fa', it would have been an apparent connection. [The difference has become clear between the speech of God, who knows the causes and what is connected to them of effects, which His noblest creation ﷺ was commanded to, in Surat al-An'am and az-Zumar, and the speech related from His prophet Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, in this surah.] ﴿Who﴾, meaning: which of us, or the one ﴿to whom there comes a punishment that disgraces him﴾. Since the content of their saying ﴿We do not understand much of what you say﴾ [Hud: 91] included the attribution of lying, because speaking what has no correspondence in reality that matches it is lying, He said: ﴿and who is a liar﴾, meaning: from me and from you. So the estimate: if "man" is a relative pronoun, you will know who is disgraced by the punishment and the lie, I or you; and if it is interrogative: which of us will be reached by a punishment that disgraces him, and which of us is a liar. So remain in your position and do not advance beyond it. ﴿And wait﴾, meaning: await what will be among its consequences.

Since they were calling him a liar and denying his words, he emphasized, saying: ﴿Indeed, I am with you a watcher﴾, for the same purpose. I have only estimated this preceding phrase to separate the speech in His saying "sawfa" [You will know]; it is permissible to coordinate it with "u'malu" [act]. He used the bare form and did not say "murtaqib" [one who watches], indicating that his concern is striving in the work commanded by God, because he is exaggerating in awaiting the outcome with them, in contempt of them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 94:

Since it was as if it had been said: "They took the statement at its face value, did not benefit from its piercing warning and its overwhelming threat, and persisted in the ugliness they were engaged in until Our command came at the appointed term set for them," [the verse] said, conjoining it to that, and the conjunction was with *wa* (and) (p-367) because no threat had preceded with a specific time, as in the stories of Salih and Lut, peace be upon them, after which the coming is caused by it and follows it: ﴿And when Our command came﴾, meaning the attachment of Our will to the punishment. ﴿We saved﴾ by what We have of greatness ﴿Shu'ayb﴾, meaning a great salvation, ﴿and those who believed﴾ being ﴿with him﴾ among them, and from what We punished them with. Our deliverance of them was ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾. And when he mentioned the salvation of the believers, he followed it with the destruction of the disbelievers, so he said: ﴿And the cry seized those who did wrong﴾, meaning those who committed wrong and did not repent. ﴿The cry﴾: and it seems it was less than the cry of Thamud, because they were weaker than them, so for this reason the sign of feminine gender was made manifest in this [case] and not in that one.

When he mentioned the cry, he mentioned what resulted from it, so he said: ﴿So they became in their homes prostrate﴾, meaning at the time when a person expects joy and every good, ﴿in their homes, lying prostrate﴾, meaning fallen, remaining in their place.

Since prostration (al-juthum) cannot occur through death alone, he clarified the intended meaning of His words ﴿as though they had never lived therein﴾, that is: they did not dwell in their homes as wealthy people who move about freely, going back and forth among the beautiful women, amusing themselves with song. And since the content of that is distance (al-ib'ad), he emphasized it with His words ﴿Away with Madyan!﴾, a distance, though it has the meaning of the opposite of nearness; with it comes destruction, so it is from ba'ida with a kasra. And he confirmed what I understood, that their affair was lighter than the affair of Thamud, with His words ﴿just as Thamud was removed﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 96:

Since Shu'ayb was the father-in-law (khatan) of Musa, peace be upon them both, the mention of his story here was expected, given what prompted that expectation: the mention of his Book at the beginning of the surah, and what is in the staff of Musa of the correspondence with the story of the she-camel of those who were sealed with the simile of their condition. So He mentioned it after them, opening it with the particle of expectation (harf al-tawaqqu'). He said, emphasizing, as an alert that Pharaoh did the same as the Quraysh did in turning away from the great signs, and Musa, peace be upon him, did not leave anything of what was revealed to him of his warning: ﴿And We indeed sent﴾. He repeated the verb and made it manifest in the aspect of greatness, as an indication of his dazzling miracles. ﴿Musa with Our signs﴾, that is, the miracles which He manifested. ﴿And clear authority﴾, that is: a compelling command over the Copts. And it is apparent that this is a report of Musa, peace be upon him, from him, according to what he had of overbearing force and of burning anger against him. ﴿Manifest﴾, that is: clear in itself, and in its strength of clarity it is as if it makes manifest to others what is in it of secrets. The word "ayah" (sign) covers both the indicator (amarah) and the decisive proof (dalil qati'), while "sultan" (authority) is specific to the decisive proof, and "mubin" (manifest) [is specific to] what contains clarity.

ill translate this faithfully.

**To Pharaoh** the tyrant of the Copts **and his chiefs**, i.e., the nobles of his people, whom the followers trail behind, because the greatest aim was to remove their hands from the Children of Israel.

Since the one who counsels himself is the one who follows no one except in what he knows to be right, he expressed wonder at the chiefs, pointing to the speed of their denial of the clear signs and their following in what its error is not hidden from anyone who has a grain of sense: **﴿So they followed﴾**, i.e., as a consequence of this manifest matter, Pharaoh disobeyed, and his chiefs drove their own souls to follow our will in that, from among them, **﴿the command of Pharaoh﴾** [i.e., everything they understood him to desire and to command], and the lowly followed them, so they closed ranks in opposition, except for whomever God willed from among them. **﴿And not﴾**, i.e., while the reality is that **﴿the command of Pharaoh was rightly guided﴾**, i.e., sound. Along with this, the sequence after mentioning Thamud contains a reminder of the two signs of the she-camel and the staff, an indication of the power to resurrect mentioned at the beginning of the surah, whose fear compels every good, just as this was also among the benefits of placing the story of Abraham after the story of Salih, peace be upon them both. He limited himself here to mentioning Pharaoh and his people because the purpose of these stories, as previously stated, is to strengthen (the Prophet) in confronting opposition by conveying the warning, even if the aversion of those who convey it intensifies and the number of followers among them is small, and that nothing of it should be left out out of fear of their persistence or their turning away, nor hope of their turning toward it and the abundance of their believers. This is the condition of the family of Pharaoh. As for the Children of Israel, they hesitated only out of fear of Pharaoh at the outset, then all of them closed ranks in following, then after that they would change every little while, not out of aversion to the warning but for other reasons among the matters and wondrous decrees, as explained in their stories. **Al-mala'** (the chiefs): the nobles whose dignity fills the hearts upon seeing them. **Al-ittiba'** (following): seeking the second to act according to the action of the first in whatever direction is taken, and it may be out of aversion, unlike obedience. **Al-amr** (command): a demand in the form of "do," and it implies the will of the one commanded to the thing commanded in general, though the exact obedience of the commanded may not be intended. **Al-rashid** (rightly guided): the one who leads to good and guides to it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 98:

Then he made clear the lack of rectitude in the affair of Pharaoh by His saying: ﴿He will lead his people﴾, that is, those who had the power of resistance ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾, and they will be following him as they followed him in the world. He indicated, by using the form that should be the present tense in the past tense, the certainty of its occurrence, as one who has certainly occurred and passed, so He said: ﴿and he will bring them into the Fire﴾, meaning: just as he brought them to its water (ghiṭā'uhā, i.e., the sea) in the world. Since the implied sense was: "then wretched are those who come to water," He followed it with an explanation of the verb and the object, so He said: ﴿And wretched is the watering place to which they are brought﴾, as the sea, when they came to it, was the most wretched watering place any person ever came to, because a watering place is sought to quench thirst and cool the hearts, whereas this produces the opposite of that.

When Pharaoh was described as having great estate, numerous troops and wealth, and a vast kingdom, God, exalted is He, belittled his worldly life by belittling all of the world that is part of it. He dropped it from the mention, being content with pointing to it, and did not affirm it, unlike in the story of ʿAd. So He said: ﴿And they were followed﴾, using the passive form, because what is being reported is the action itself, not who performs it. ﴿In this﴾, that is, in this base life, ﴿a curse﴾. So they are cursed in it by every one who curses, from among the Muslims and others from among the people of the religions. Thus the curse of God is upon those who made their condition seem fair and approved their misguidance, in order to lead astray the servants from among the people of *ilhad* (heresy, deviation from the truth), through the trial of *ittihad* (the heretical doctrine of union with God). ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection﴾ also, they will be cursed by those who curse them. Even the close friends of *ittihad* will, on that Day, be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing. Then He explained what the hearer of this should say, with His words: ﴿Evil is the gift that is given﴾, that is, the following that is followed and the aid that is aided. The curse is a follower of their punishment in this world and is followed by [the curse] in the Hereafter, and the punishment is a gift (*rifd*) for it, and it is a gift for the punishment. The root *r-f-d* revolves around the meaning of following. Or the intended meaning is that their cursing continues without cease, one thing following another, so every curse that follows some form of disgrace, whether punishment or cursing, is followed by a curse added to it. This is called a *rifd*, and it is in truth a form of aid, in the manner of their saying: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

The meaning of ﴿He will go before﴾ [Hud: 98] is that he will be in front of them, not driving them, but they will be following his trail one after another, so their entry into the Fire will be together. *Al-qiyama* means rising from death for the reckoning. *Al-itbaʿ* means seeking the second to catch up with the first, however it proceeds. *Al-laʿn* from God means removal from mercy by judging it so, and from the servants it means invoking it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 100:

Since these reports are of the utmost gravity in warning, which none but one deeply learned in knowledge could grasp, it is certain and known that he (ﷺ) did not bring them except from Allah, for it is evident that he had never studied any knowledge nor had he ever sat with a scholar at any time. Moreover, [these reports] contain various kinds of eloquence, embody modes of excellent expression, and point, through the fine arrangement of their contexts, to the varieties of wisdom and the benefits of their detailed explanations across the branches of knowledge. Therefore they deserve to be referred to with the demonstrative of distance, signifying the remoteness of their rank and the loftiness of their matter. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That﴾, i.e., the great news and the momentous affair, ﴿is among the reports of the towns﴾ (p-372). He reinforced this meaning by the word "naba'" (report), because a naba' is a report whose content is of great importance, and from it comes "nabi" (prophet). By using the present tense in His words ﴿We relate it to you﴾, He indicated that just as We have related them to you in this state for the aforementioned purpose, We will relate them to you for other purposes among the various aspects of eloquence and the diverse forms of wisdom, as you will see when they are narrated. Then He indicated, by what He stated about their remains in His words ﴿Of them some are standing and some are reaped﴾, i.e., of the towns, that just as you heard what We related of their affair with your ears and retained it in your heart, you perceive it with your eye by observing their buildings and traces, standing and reaped, i.e., ruined, with nothing of their structures left except some of their walls.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 101:

Since the stories earlier in this surah contain the most severe warning and the greatest threat for whoever has insight, he (al-Biqa'i) made explicit to those hardened of heart that what makes their destruction necessary is only wrongdoing (ẓulm). So God, the Exalted, said, linking this to what might be said: "We did such-and-such to them and informed you of it": ﴿We did not wrong them﴾ in any part of it, ﴿but they wronged themselves﴾, relying on their equals (andād), turning away from Our presence, feeling secure from Our punishment, so We seized them. ﴿Then﴾, meaning: the result of their reliance on other than Us was that ﴿they did not avail them﴾, meaning: in any way whatsoever, ﴿their gods to whom﴾ (and He depicted their past state, saying): ﴿they called upon﴾, meaning: they had called upon them and continued in their calling upon them until the time of the seizing. [And He made clear the baseness of their rank, saying]: ﴿besides God﴾, meaning the One who possesses all the attributes of perfection (ṣifāt al-kamāl). He mentioned the object of "did avail" in a negated, generalized form, saying: ﴿anything﴾, meaning: even if it were small. ﴿When there came the command﴾, meaning: the punishment of ﴿your Lord﴾, meaning the One who did good to you by delaying the punishment that would uproot your community, and who made you a prophet of mercy. ﴿And they added to them nothing﴾ in their states which they had before worshipping them ﴿but ruin﴾, meaning: destruction and loss. For they were among those whose success was hoped for, but when they became entangled in worshipping them, got stuck in their error, and moved away from uprightness through their misguidance, they lost their own selves, which are the capital; so how could they then gain profits?

Qaṣṣ (narrating) means following a trace, so here it means reporting events that follow one another. Du'ā' (calling/invoking) means a seeker's request for an action from another, and calling out to a thing by its name with a particle of address; both meanings are intended. And ﴿besides God﴾ indicates a rank lower than the rank of worshipping God, because it is of the lesser, and it is the closer to the direction of the bottom (al-sufl). Tabb means destruction and loss.

When the aim of all this was to strike the hearts of the Arabs with the arrows of warning, so that they might give up the blindness of *taqlid* (blind imitation), He, the Exalted, said, informing that the One who befell those people for their wrongdoing, and who lies in wait for every wrongdoer whether he wrongs himself or others:

﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord﴾, that is, a seizing of such magnitude like it, ﴿when He seizes the cities﴾, which He mentioned with the attribute of beneficence, showing the kindness He has toward him, so that he would not fear for his people such a seizing. That is, [He seizes] their inhabitants, even if they were not those whose report has already preceded, and even if they were great in number and multitude. But reporting about the cities is more terrifying, because it conveys that destruction may encompass them on account of their people, out of intense anger at their deeds, as with the cities of the people of Lot, peace be upon him, ﴿while they are wrongdoers﴾. Al-Bukhari (*Tafsir*) related from Abu Musa, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited: ﴿And thus is the seizing of your Lord﴾, to the end of the verse.

Since such a seizer is not approached by any creature and no angel is able to overpower Him, it was most fitting to follow that with His saying: ﴿Indeed His seizing is painful﴾, that is, afflicting, cutting off hopes, filling the body, the spirit and the soul with punishment, ﴿severe﴾, that is, difficult, crushing the powers. Perhaps He mentioned here the name of the Lord, adding it to the one addressed by these reports, and repeating it in this context, where the mind might have otherwise leapt to the names al-Jabbar (the Compeller) or al-Muntaqim (the Avenger) as more suitable, as an indication that He, glorified is He, will nurture you in the best nurturing: by making you prevail over the whole religion, by the submission of the great to your command, by the humbling of the mighty before your authority, and by the lowering of heads before the loftiness of your station. Therefore, do not burden yourself with seeking to answer them by sending down a sign, or by abandoning what angers them of warning and the like. And Allah is the Granter of success.

ولَمّا كانَ مِمّا جَرَّ هَذِهِ القِصَصَ وهَذِهِ المَواعِظَ تَكْذِيبُهم لِما يُوعَدُونَ [p. 375] مِنَ العَذابِ النّاشِئِ عَنْ إنْكارِ البَعْثِ المَذْكُورِ في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿ولَئِنْ قُلْتَ إنَّكم مَبْعُوثُونَ مِن بَعْدِ المَوْتِ﴾ [هود: ٧] - الآياتِ. أشارَ تَعالى إلى تَحَقُّقِ أمْرِ الآخِرَةِ وأنَّهُ مِمّا يَنْبَغِي الِاهْتِمامُ بِهِ رَدًّا لِلْمَقْطَعِ عَلى المَطْلَعِ، وإعْلامًا بِأنَّهُ لا فَرْقَ بَيْنَهُ وبَيْنَ ما تَحَقَّقَ إيقاعُهُ مِن عَذابِ هَذِهِ الأُمَمِ في القُدْرَةِ عَلَيْهِ بِقَوْلِهِ مُؤَكَّدًا لِأجْلِ جُحُودِهِمْ أنْ يَكُونَ في شَيْءٍ مِمّا مَضى دَلالَةٌ عَلَيْهِ بِوَجْهٍ مِنَ الوُجُوهِ: ﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ﴾ أيِ النَّبَأِ العَظِيمِ والقَصَصِ والوَعْظِ بِما يُذْكَرُ ﴿لآيَةً﴾ أيْ: لَعَلامَةً عَظِيمَةً ودَلالَةً بَتَّةً. ولَمّا كانَ وُجُودُ الشَّيْءِ عَدَمًا بِالنِّسْبَةِ إلى ما لا نَفْعَ لَهُ بِهِ، قالَ: ﴿لِمَن خافَ عَذابَ﴾ يَوْمِ الحَياةِ ﴿الآخِرَةِ﴾ لِأنَّهُ نَفْعٌ خاصٌّ بِهِ، وإنَّما كانَ آيَةً لَهُ لِأنَّهُ إذا نَظَرَ إلى إهْلاكِهِ لِلظّالِمِينَ إهْلاكًا عامًّا بِسَبَبِ ظُلْمِهِمْ وإنْجائِهِ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ، عَلِمَ أنَّهُ قادِرٌ عَلى ما يُرِيدُ، وأنَّهُ لا بُدَّ أنْ يُجازِيَ كُلًّا بِما فَعَلَ، فَإذا رَأى أنَّ ظُلْمَهُ كَثِيرِينَ يَمُوتُونَ بِغَيْرِ انْتِقامٍ عَلِمَ أنَّهُ لا بُدَّ مِن يَوْمٍ يُجازِيهِمْ فِيهِ، وهو اليَوْمُ الَّذِي أخْبَرَتْ بِهِ عَنْهُ رُسُلُهُ، وزادَ في الإشارَةِ إلى تَهْوِيلِهِ بِإعادَةِ اسْمِ الإشارَةِ (ism al-ishara, the demonstrative noun) في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ أيِ اليَوْمُ العَظِيمُ الَّذِي يَكُونُ فِيهِ عَذابُ الآخِرَةِ ﴿يَوْمٌ﴾ وأشارَ - إلى يُسْرِ البَعْثِ وسُهُولَتِهِ عَلَيْهِ وأنَّهُ [أمْرٌ ثابِتٌ] لا بُدَّ مِنهُ - بِاسْمِ المَفْعُولِ (ism al-maf'ul, the passive participle) مِن قَوْلِهِ: ﴿مَجْمُوعٌ لَهُ﴾ أيْ: لِإظْهارِ العَدْلِ فِيهِ [p. 376] والفَضْلِ ﴿النّاسُ﴾ أيْ: كُلُّ مَن فِيهِ أهْلِيَّةُ التَّحَرُّكِ والِاضْطِرابِ، وما ثَمَّ يَوْمٌ غَيْرُهُ يَكُونُ بِهَذِهِ الصِّفَةِ أصْلًا.

ولَمّا لَمْ يَسْبِقُهُ يَوْمٌ اجْتَمَعَ فِيهِ جَمِيعُ الخَلْقِ مِنَ الجِنِّ والإنْسِ والمَلائِكَةِ وجَمِيعُ الحَيَواناتِ أحْياءً، وكانَ ذَلِكَ مُسَوِّغًا لِأنْ تُعَدَّ شَهادَةُ غَيْرِهِ عَدَمًا فَقالَ تَعالى: ﴿وذَلِكَ﴾ أيِ اليَوْمُ العَظِيمُ ﴿يَوْمٌ مَشْهُودٌ﴾ أيْ: هو نَفْسُهُ لَهم ولِغَيْرِهِمْ مِن جَمِيعِ الخَلْقِ، فَيَكُونُ تَنْوِينُهُ (tanwin, nunation) لِلتَّعْظِيمِ بِدَلالَةِ المَقامِ، أوْ يَكُونُ المَعْنى أنَّهُ أهْلٌ لِأنْ يُشْهَدَ، وتَتَوَفَّرَ الدَّواعِي عَلى حُضُورِهِ لِما فِيهِ مِن عَجائِبِ الأُمُورِ والأهْوالِ العِظامِ والمَواقِفِ الصَّعْبَةِ، فَلا يَكُونُ ثَمَّ شُغْلٌ إلّا نَظَرُ ما فِيهِ والإحاطَةُ بِحَوادِثِهِ خَوْفَ التَّلافِ ورَجاءَ الخَلاصِ؛ والآيَةُ: العَلامَةُ العَظِيمَةُ لِما فِيها مِنَ البَيانِ عَنِ الأمْرِ الكَبِيرِ؛ والخَوْفُ: انْزِعاجُ النَّفْسِ بِتَوَقُّعِ الشَّرِّ، وضِدُّهُ الأمْنُ وهو سُكُونُ النَّفْسِ بِتَوَقُّعِ الخَيْرِ؛ والعَذابُ: اسْتِمْرارُ الألَمِ.

When their saying ﴿What holds it back?﴾ [Hud: 8] had preceded, it was as if it were said in reply to them: We are able to hasten it, and it, as we have pointed out in this verse, is with Us, whenever We wish, in the utmost ease. ﴿And We do not delay it﴾, that is, the Day or the recompense, despite Our greatness and complete power to bring into existence anything of things, ﴿except for a term﴾, that is, for the arrival of an end-term ﴿counted﴾, whose determination was decreed in eternity by One whose word is not changed in His presence, and before whose judgment everything stands. So He does not fear that anything will escape Him.

The root *ʾajal* (ajal, "term, appointed time") with its four permutations, *ʾajala*, *jaʾala*, *jalaʾa* and *lajaʾa*, all revolves around a fixed period set for a thing. The *ajal* (term), with a vowelled *a*, is the duration of a thing and the limit of a time, in death and in the falling due of a debt, by naming the part after the whole. *Taʾjil* (fixing a term) is determining the *ajal*, and it entails delay. From it comes *ʾajila al-shayʾu* (the thing was delayed), like *fariḥa*, when it was late. *Al-ājila* is the *ākhira* (the Hereafter). *Ajala al-shayʾa* (with *fatḥa*) means to detain and prevent it, because the *ajal* holds back and prevents what is termed. From it comes *ajlā*, like *jamzā*, which is a known pasture for them, as if its goodness detains the shepherd in it. *Ajala al-sharra ʿalayhim* means he stirred up, aroused and provoked evil against them. *Ajala li-ahlihi* means he earned, gathered and schemed for his family, because all of that is among the necessary features of one who has a term, or the meaning is that he brought about the term of that. Like *maqʿad* and *muʿẓam*, *mustanqaʿ al-māʾ* (stagnant water) is the pool, because it surrounds the water as the term surrounds the termed. *Ajjalahu fīhi taʾjīlan* means he gathered it, so it was gathered. *Al-maʾjal* is the basin in which water is held. *Ajjalū mā lahum* means they detained their property in the pasture. *Al-ajil* (with *kasra*) is a herd of wild cattle, likened to it in its gathering, since it is most protective for it, as a term is a fortress, as it has been said, "a strong fortress." *Al-ajil* (also with *kasra*) is a pain in the neck, because it is among the causes of the arrival of the term. *Ajjalahu* means he treated him for it. With *ḍamma*, it is the plural of *ajīl*, for the one who is late and for what has gathered of clay placed around the palm tree, because it surrounds it as a term surrounds, and protects it. *Taʾajjala al-qawm* means the people gathered, because gathering is more protective for them. *Ajal* (with two *fatḥa*s followed by sukūn) is an answer like *naʿam* in form and meaning, except that it is better than it in confirmation, while *naʿam* is better than it in interrogation. The reality of this statement is the report that the *ajal*, that is, the time of that act which requires it or about which the question is asked, has arrived. *Faʿaltu dhālika ajlaka* (without *min*), *min ajlika*, and *min ajlāka* [and *min ajalālika*] are said, and it is pronounced with *kasra* in all of them, that is, *min jallika*. This is what the *Qamus* (the lexicon) says. In the section on the letter *jīm* it says: "*Faʿaltuhu min jullika*" (with *ḍamma*), "*wa-jalālika*" and "*wa-jallika*" (with *fatḥa*), "*wa-tajillatika*" and "*wa-ijlālika*" (with *kasra*), and "*min ajli ijlālika*" and "*min ajlika*" have the same meaning. End of quotation.

The reality of it is that *faʿaltu* is the subject of *min ajalika* (with *fatḥa*), or the *min* is causal, meaning your *ajal* is the cause of it. Were it not for your existence, I would not have done it, so it is for your glorification. *Al-maljaʾ* and *al-laja'* (with *fatḥa*) are the refuge and the shelter, as if it were likened to the *ajal*. From it comes *lajaʾa ilayhi* (with *kasra* or *fatḥa*, like *manaʿa* and *faraḥa*), meaning he sought refuge. *Alja'a amrahu ilā Allāh* means he entrusted his affair to God. *Alja'a fulānan ilā kadhā* means he compelled him to it. *Al-talʾija* is coercion. *Al-laja'* (with *fatḥa*) is the frog, because of its seeking refuge in the water. From this comes *al-jaʾal* (like *ṣayqal*), and *jaʾal* and *jaʾala* are both prohibited, and *Jīl* without the *hamza*, all of it is the name of the hyena, because of its frequent resorting to its den. From it comes *jaʾila* (like *faraḥa*) *jaʾalānan*, meaning he limped. It is as if it were a likeness of its gait, because among its names is "the lame one." Or it is a likeness of the gait of one who climbs the steps of the *maljaʾ*, that is, the fortress. Likewise *al-uʾajjal* (like *qinnab* and *qubbar*), which is the male of the wild goats, because its horns are like a fortress for it. *Jaʾīlat al-jurḥ* is its pus, which is its discharge, because it is among the causes of the nearness of the term. Likewise *al-ijtiʾlāl*, that is, fear, may be a cause of that (p. 379), and may be a cause of hastening toward the fortress. *Jaʾala* (like *manaʿa*) means he went and came. *Al-ṣūf* (wool): he gathered it and it gathered, intransitive and transitive, all of which are among the necessary features of the *ajal* in the sense of duration. *Jalaʾa bi-l-rajul* (like *manaʿa*) means he threw him down, and *bi-thawbihi* means he threw it. It is as if he made him in the strength of one whose term has come. If you wish to put this in order, say: the root, while revolving around duration, sometimes looks at duration itself, sometimes at its end, sometimes at its extension and delay, sometimes at what brings it near, sometimes at its benefit, and sometimes at what is necessary within it. From looking at duration itself: *taʾjīl*, in the sense of fixing the term, which is the duration of a thing; *faʿaltu hādhā min ajlika*, meaning were it not for your existence I would not have done it; and *ajal*, in the sense of *naʿam*, meaning the duration of the act has arrived. From looking at the end: *dana al-ajal*, the term drew near, in death and debt. From looking at delay: *ajila al-shayʾ*, when it was late, and *al-ājila*, the Hereafter. From looking at the near cause: *al-ajil* (with *kasra*), for a pain in the neck; *jaʾīlat al-jurḥ*, for its pus, that is, its discharge; *jalaʾa bi-l-rajul*, he threw him down, and *bi-thawbihi*, he threw it; *ajala al-sharra ʿalayhim*, he earned it, or aroused and provoked it; and *al-ijtiʾlāl*, fear. From looking at the benefit, which is that *taʾjīl*, the fixing of a term for a thing, prevents taking it before the period set for it: *al-ajil* (with *kasra*) for the herd of wild cattle; *ajjala al-shayʾ*, he detained and prevented it; *ajlā*, like *jamzā*, a known pasture for them (p. 380); *taʾajjala al-qawm*, the people gathered; *jaʾala al-ṣūf*, he gathered wool; *al-lajāʾ* and *al-maljaʾ*, the refuge and the shelter; the frog, because of its staying by its refuge from the water; *al-jaʾal* for the hyena, because of its staying by its den; and *jaʾila*, like *faraḥa*, he limped, as it is likened to its gait, because it is called "the lame one." *Al-uʾajjal*, like *qinnab* and *qubbar*, for the male of the wild goats, because of its fortifying itself by its horns. *Al-ujul* (with *ḍamma*) is what has gathered of clay placed around the palm tree; *al-maʾājil* is the basin in which water is held, and a stagnant pool in general; *ajjalahu taʾjīlan*, he gathered it. From looking at what is necessary within the duration: *ajjala li-ahlihi*, he earned, gathered, brought and schemed for his family; and *jaʾala*, like *manaʿa*, he came and went. Thus it has become clear that what is meant by *ajal* here is *ḥīn* (a time, a due moment).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 105:

Since it was as if it were said: "Would that I knew what the condition of people will be when that term comes, and among them are the tyrants, the leaders, and those of great stature and eminence!" He answered with His words: ﴿On the day it comes﴾, meaning: that term—they will not be able to speak against it, nor even to speak at all. Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah omitted the yāʾ (of yawma yaʾti), making do with the kasrah in its place, as is common in the dialect of Hudhayl. This indicates that the severity of its terror prevents the people of the Standing (al-mawqif) from speaking at all for about two-thirds of it. Then they are permitted to speak in the remaining third, by the indication of the omitted letter and the evidence of the exception (istithnaʾ), since it is customary for the excepted part to be less than the part from which it is excepted. ﴿No soul will speak﴾, even the least speech, as indicated by the deletion of the tāʾ (lā tukallamu), ﴿except by His permission﴾, from all of creation on that day (p-381), which is the Day of the Hereafter, and it is the container of this term. It is a very long day, of varied kinds, arts, terrors and affairs: at times they are permitted to speak; at times seals are placed upon their mouths; at times fear, regret and pains silence them; and at times dispute and contention make them speak. ﴿Except by His permission﴾, that is, by the permission of your Lord, whose mention is repeated in these verses, indicating the excellence of His nurture and the perfection of His management.

Since it is known from this that it is a day of greatness and dominance, the division of those present is consequent upon that greatness. So He said: ﴿Among them is the wretched﴾, that is, among the creatures present for His command, one for whom wretchedness has been established, so he was facilitated in the world for its deeds; ﴿and the happy﴾, one for whom happiness has been established, so he walked according to its pattern. Al-ta'khir (delay) is removing a thing from its direction by distancing it from it, and its opposite is al-taqdim (advancement). Al-ajal is the appointed time for the occurrence of one of the matters. The lam denotes cause, purpose and wisdom, unlike "ila" (to). Al-shaqa' is the strength of the causes of affliction.

Since the Qur'anic verses appear in the text, I should note that the Qur'anic quotations are given in the translation below, with their meanings rendered in English.

Since most of creation is destined for destruction, and the setting is one of warning and terror, the Exalted began with the wretched, arranging the dissemination (of the account) in the same order as the folding, so He said: ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾, meaning: those whom hardship and severity have overtaken, ﴿then they will be in the Fire﴾, meaning: it is decreed for them that they will enter the Fire, which is the Fire that, if you knew, ﴿for them therein will be groaning﴾, meaning: very great indeed, ﴿and wailing﴾. (The verb) zafara means to expel one's breath after drawing it in, while shahiqa means that weeping recurs in the chest. This is what al-Qamus says. Ibn Kathir said, in his commentary on Surat al-Anbiya': al-zafir is the expulsion of their breaths, and al-shahiq is the drawing in of their breaths. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that al-zafir is the intense sound and al-shahiq is the weak sound. It is related from al-Dahhak and Muqatil that al-zafir is the first part of a donkey's bray, and al-shahiq is its last part, when it finishes its sound and draws it back into its belly. The words of al-Rummani on this will come later. ﴿Abiding therein﴾, meaning: without cessation. He expressed this by His saying, following the Arabic manner of speech: ﴿for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾.

Since everything belongs to Him, and nothing in Him is ugly, and He is capable of everything, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ [meaning: a duration that He wills; for He does not decree for them that they will remain in it, so they do not enter it].

Since the circumstances of this surah call for consoling the Prophet ﷺ regarding what the Exalted informed him of in His saying: ﴿So perhaps you will leave out part of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud: 12], and so on, from the constriction of his breast, and for this reason these narratives were brought, as the explanation of this has passed, He expressed (it) by the name of the Lord, indicating that He is good to him in everything that gladdens his heart and expands his breast, so He said: ﴿your Lord﴾. People have proceeded with this exception according to its apparent meaning, and then they prolonged their disagreement over identifying the excepted duration. What has become clear to me, and Allah knows best, is that when the certainty of eternal abiding in both abodes was repeated, and that association (with Allah) is not forgiven, while faith necessitates Paradise, it might be supposed that nothing else is possible, as the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) supposed, especially when one considers the definitive wording in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], alongside His restricting the forgiveness of other than that by will, in His saying: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. (p. 383) This exception came to make known that the matter in it rests with Allah, the Exalted, like other matters: He may do in all of them what He wills, even if He has firmly stated the matter, but what He has informed of does not occur otherwise. This is like your saying: "Dwell in this house for your lifetime, except what Zayd wills," while Zayd may will nothing at all. Just as the conditioning by the permanence of the heavens and the earth is not intended in its apparent sense, so too the exception: Allah does not will to end abiding for any of the two groups. Stating it in this manner is more indicative of power and greater in investing (one with) the favor. Then I saw that the Imam Abu Ahmad al-Baghawi had mentioned the meaning of this at the end of what he cited in his commentary of the sayings concerning the verse, and something similar was reported from al-Farra'. He illustrated it with your saying: "By Allah, I will strike you unless I see otherwise," while your resolve is to strike him. Al-Tahawi, in Bayan al-Mushkil, attributed it to the people of language, among them al-Farra'.

Since the eternal abiding of the disbelievers is part of the judgment with justice between the two groups, because it is among the greatest of the blessings of the believers who opposed them for the sake of Allah, as was previously pointed out at the beginning of Surat Yunus, peace be upon him, at His saying: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾ [Yunus: 4], it might have been supposed that if the exception were taken in its apparent sense, their removal from the Fire would not be at a (fixed) time. He negated this supposition by His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you, ﴿is an effector of what He intends﴾, meaning: it is not permissible for Him to begin a reversal from what He has willed, nor to prevent His will, nor is anything from it beyond His reach, despite the multitude of things willed. So there is no objection to Him, and nothing is obligatory upon Him for anyone. Rather, He may cause the disobedient to abide in Paradise and cause (p. 384) the obedient to abide in the Fire. But just as that is established so that it may be believed, because it is an attribute of perfection, it is also established that He, glorified is He, does not do that, and His word is not changed in His presence, because that too is among the attributes of perfection. Moreover, closing the verse with this includes a hope for the people of the Fire regarding their removal from it, (though) an increase in their punishment.
