He expressed this by His saying, following the Arabic manner of speech: ﴿for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾.

Since everything belongs to Him, and nothing in Him is ugly, and He is capable of everything, He indicated this by His saying: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ [meaning: a duration that He wills; for He does not decree for them that they will remain in it, so they do not enter it].

Since the circumstances of this surah call for consoling the Prophet ﷺ regarding what the Exalted informed him of in His saying: ﴿So perhaps you will leave out part of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud: 12], and so on, from the constriction of his breast, and for this reason these narratives were brought, as the explanation of this has passed, He expressed (it) by the name of the Lord, indicating that He is good to him in everything that gladdens his heart and expands his breast, so He said: ﴿your Lord﴾. People have proceeded with this exception according to its apparent meaning, and then they prolonged their disagreement over identifying the excepted duration. What has become clear to me, and Allah knows best, is that when the certainty of eternal abiding in both abodes was repeated, and that association (with Allah) is not forgiven, while faith necessitates Paradise, it might be supposed that nothing else is possible, as the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) supposed, especially when one considers the definitive wording in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with﴾ [al-Nisa': 48], alongside His restricting the forgiveness of other than that by will, in His saying: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. (p. 383) This exception came to make known that the matter in it rests with Allah, the Exalted, like other matters: He may do in all of them what He wills, even if He has firmly stated the matter, but what He has informed of does not occur otherwise. This is like your saying: "Dwell in this house for your lifetime, except what Zayd wills," while Zayd may will nothing at all. Just as the conditioning by the permanence of the heavens and the earth is not intended in its apparent sense, so too the exception: Allah does not will to end abiding for any of the two groups. Stating it in this manner is more indicative of power and greater in investing (one with) the favor. Then I saw that the Imam Abu Ahmad al-Baghawi had mentioned the meaning of this at the end of what he cited in his commentary of the sayings concerning the verse, and something similar was reported from al-Farra'. He illustrated it with your saying: "By Allah, I will strike you unless I see otherwise," while your resolve is to strike him. Al-Tahawi, in Bayan al-Mushkil, attributed it to the people of language, among them al-Farra'.

Since the eternal abiding of the disbelievers is part of the judgment with justice between the two groups, because it is among the greatest of the blessings of the believers who opposed them for the sake of Allah, as was previously pointed out at the beginning of Surat Yunus, peace be upon him, at His saying: ﴿that He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾ [Yunus: 4], it might have been supposed that if the exception were taken in its apparent sense, their removal from the Fire would not be at a (fixed) time. He negated this supposition by His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you, ﴿is an effector of what He intends﴾, meaning: it is not permissible for Him to begin a reversal from what He has willed, nor to prevent His will, nor is anything from it beyond His reach, despite the multitude of things willed. So there is no objection to Him, and nothing is obligatory upon Him for anyone. Rather, He may cause the disobedient to abide in Paradise and cause (p. 384) the obedient to abide in the Fire. But just as that is established so that it may be believed, because it is an attribute of perfection, it is also established that He, glorified is He, does not do that, and His word is not changed in His presence, because that too is among the attributes of perfection. Moreover, closing the verse with this includes a hope for the people of the Fire regarding their removal from it, (though) an increase in their punishment.

When the affair of the wretched was complete, He followed it with its counterpart, saying: ﴿And as for those who were made happy﴾, that is, who attained their aims and whose affair was made easy, ﴿then they will be in the Garden﴾, that is, the one that has become known by necessity from the religion, ﴿abiding therein﴾ constantly, forever, ﴿for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, according to the usage of the Arabs in expressing perpetuity without any end, as in such cases, ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾. The clearest proof for what I have said about the istithna' (exception) is His saying: ﴿a gift (ʿaṭāʾan)﴾, which is in the accusative (naṣb) as a maṣdar (verbal noun), ﴿never cut off (ghayra majdhūdh)﴾, that is, uninterrupted [nor broken, nor separated, as a gift among gifts, nor scattered, nor held in contempt]. For if they were to be separated from the bliss, in reality or in meaning, even for a moment, it would be cut off [or diminished]. In concluding with this, there is a affirmation of permanence that gives reassurance to the people of the Garden and an increase in their bliss, the opposite of what was the case for the people of the Fire.

Abu al-Hasan al-Rummani said: The zafir is the repeating of breath along with a sound until the ribs swell; its root meaning is intensity, from "a creature with a strong frame." The zafr is carrying a load on the back because of its heaviness, and a zafr is also a master, because he can bear the hardships. And the fire "zafarat" when you hear a sound from it in the intensity of its blazing. The shahiq is a terrible sound that comes out from the belly with the prolonging of breath; its root meaning is excessive length, from their saying "a shāhiq mountain," meaning one that is inaccessible in height (p-385). The khālid is that which exists in a thing forever, and the dā'im is that which remains forever; for this reason God, exalted is He, is described as Dā'im, not Khālid.

When God had informed him of the judgment that will separate people on the Day of Witnessing into the two groups mentioned, according to the ruling explained, warning and encouraging, that was sufficient for steadfastness in God's command and for persisting in carrying out everything he had been sent with, even if it was difficult, relying on help on that day in the presence of those multitudes. This was a reason for forbidding anxiety about anything, however great its impact and however grave its matter. So He said: ﴿So do not﴾. Since what this division contained was a great matter and a weighty affair, it required the soul's intense eagerness and strong longing to know what had been caused by it. This called for dropping the nūn from "kāna" (كانَ) for conciseness in speech, to hasten to the meaning [and to convey the negation of the state in its highest form]. So He said: ﴿be﴾ [i.e., in any state whatsoever] ﴿in doubt﴾. Al-mirya (المِرْيَةُ) is doubt together with the manifest evidence of accusation, as al-Rummani (الرُّمّانِيُّ) said. ﴿about what these people worship﴾, i.e., do not act like one who is in doubt, by being agitated over what they worship, persistently and renewing that at every moment, so that you would strain yourself in eagerness to hasten them to comply with the commands, by refraining from disclosing to them the harshness of warning and from seeking to answer their proposals, hoping they would desist, as has passed in His saying: ﴿so perhaps you would leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud: 12], and so on. This is because the root m-r-y, in whatever order it occurs, revolves around agitation, and it may entail casting off and separating. Ramā yarmī ramyan (رَمى يَرْمِي رَمْيًا) means he threw. Al-mirmāh (المِرْماةُ) is the hoof of a sheep, because it is cast off. Al-ramy (الرَّمْيُ) is thin pieces of cloud. Al-rīm (الرِّيمُ) is an open wasteland. Mā yarīmu yaf'alu kadhā (ما يَرِيمُ يَفْعَلُ كَذا) means he does not cease doing such. Al-rīm (الرِّيمُ) is a path because of the agitation in it. Al-qabr (القَبْرُ) is so named because it is thrown aside in a part of the earth and the dead person is cast into it. Rīma fulānun bil-makān (رِيمَ فُلانٌ بِالمَكانِ) means he stayed in the place, separated from others, as if he had thrown himself into it. Raymmatis-saḥābah (رَيَّمَتِ السَّحابَةُ), when a cloud persists and does not clear, because it is in its nature to pour rain. Maraa al-ḍar' (مَرى الضَّرْعَ) means he wiped the udder for milking. The wind murī al-saḥāb (تُمْرِي السَّحابَ) drives the clouds. Al-maryu (المَرْيُ) is the stomach, because it expels what is in it. Al-mirya (المِرْيَةُ) is doubt, that is, the wavering of belief. Al-mīrah (المِيرَةُ) is bringing in food. Then God began a statement which stands in the position of the cause for that, so He said: ﴿They worship﴾, i.e., they perform worship on a continuous basis, ﴿except as their fathers worshipped﴾. Since their worship was in a past period of time, He introduced the preposition, so He said: ﴿before﴾, i.e., they did not do that out of a doubt which, if the veil were removed from it, they would return; rather it was out of pure imitation of the fathers, while keeping in mind their being engaged in worship, as if they were present before them, watching them, while blind to looking at the proofs and arguments. This is as was the case with the nations whose reports We have related to you in imitating the fathers, equal in equality, along with their great obstinacy and intense zeal for strangers, ﴿how much more for relatives!﴾ ﴿how much more for fathers!﴾ So establish the proof against them by conveying everything We command you, just as those whose accounts We have related to you from your brother messengers did, without entertaining in mind anything of what may result from it, until what We desire of Our commands is carried out, as has preceded in the knowledge. So do not hasten, for We arrange the matter in their lowliness of station and your elevation of station, as We wish.

﴿And indeed We﴾, with the greatness We possess, ﴿will surely give them their full share﴾ of good and evil, of appointed terms and other things, and what is firmly established in a way that is not separated at all. Since fulfilling (al-tawfiyah, التَّوْفِيَةُ) may be applied to mere giving, and that may be approximate, He negated this possibility by His saying: ﴿without any diminution﴾. Al-naṣīb (النَّصِيبُ) is the portion assigned to its owner, like a share. Al-manqūṣ (المَنقُوصُ) is the quantity taken, of which a part is removed. Al-naqṣ (النَّقْصُ) is taking a part from the quantity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 110:

When He mentioned in this verse their turning away from following (him), despite what he brought of miracles and what was sent down to him of the Book, He consoled him with his brother, peace be upon them both, because when a condition is widespread it becomes lighter. He began the mention of him with the particle of expectation (harf al-tawaqquf), with what called for expecting it from the nearness of his mention with Pharaoh alongside the mention of His Book at the beginning of the surah. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book﴾ [i.e.] with what We have of greatness, ﴿Moses the Book﴾, that is, the Torah, comprehensive of good.

When the one who harms and the one who consoles was the very act of disagreement, He built the verb in the passive, saying: ﴿But it was disputed concerning it﴾, so a people believed in it and others disbelieved in it, although it is an imam and a mercy (p-388). And He, glory be to Him, wrote for him in it of every thing an admonition and a detailing of every thing. It was pleasing to the people of that time [just as your Book was disputed despite its being pleasing to the people of this time], and its clarification of guidance was the most complete clarification, as an indication that creation, however much (guidance) came to them from God—and it does not come except accompanied by decisive proofs—turned away from it and disagreed concerning it, and however much they received it from their fathers, they received it with acceptance, defended it, and gave their souls freely for it, even if it opposed reason. So the people of Moses, in their disagreement about the Book, every little while a group of them rejected some of its rulings and wanted to annul its ratification, as its explanation was mentioned more than once before from the text of the Torah and the Book of Joshua, until their affair came now to this: they became three factions—Rabbanites, Qaraites, and Samaritans—each misguiding the others. Yet with all that He did not hasten to seize them, although He was able to do so, as was done to those whose affairs were related from the nations, because of what had preceded from His judgment to delay them until the appointed term. And He separated this from the story of Moses, peace be upon him, with Pharaoh, so that together with what called for placing the preceding signs first, it would be more effective in consolation, more eloquent in comfort and solace, as is the manner of everything that is delivered to one in need little by little. ﴿And had it not been for a word﴾, that is: a great word that cannot be changed, for it is from the speech of the Greatest King, ﴿that preceded from your Lord﴾ [i.e.] the One who is good to you and to them by sending you as a mercy to the worlds, ﴿the matter would have been decided﴾, that is: the judgment would have occurred, ﴿between them﴾, that is: between those who disputed concerning (p-389) the Book of Moses, immediately; but the word preceded that the complete judgment would be on the Day of Resurrection, as He said in Surah Yunus: ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge came to them﴾ [Yunus: 93] — the verse.

When disagreement may occur without disbelief, He explained that it is with it, so He said, emphasizing because every group of the Jews denies their doubt concerning it while their action is the action of one in doubt: ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt﴾, that is: a great doubt encompassing them, ﴿concerning it﴾, that is: concerning the judgment or the Book, ﴿disquieting﴾, that is: causing suspicion, accusation and disturbance, along with what they saw of signs, among them hearing the speech of God and seeing the majesty that manifested on Mount Sinai and appeared to them in the tent of appointed time of extraordinary states.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 111:

﴿And indeed, all﴾ of those who differ concerning the truth, from the people of Musa and others, both those who are upon the truth and those who are upon falsehood. The particle "inna" (indeed), according to Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim, operates together with [its lightened form] from the heavy form, in the recitation of the others, in consideration of its origin. The "lamma" (when/indeed) in the recitation of Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and 'Asim, with shadda, is the jussive particle whose verb has been omitted. Ibn al-Hajib said: "This is common and eloquent." In the recitation of the others, with the lightened form, it is composed of the lam of commencement and "ma" which is emphatic, with negation of the opposite of what the speech affirms, so that its affirmation together with the negation of its opposite is in the most emphatic manner.

Since the condition for omitting the verb after the jussive "lamma" is that it be something expected by the occurrence of a verb before it that indicates it, the estimate is: "He will judge between them," and it will (p-390) be the meaning of what follows it with the oath particle in His saying: ﴿Surely your Lord will fully recompense them﴾, i.e., the one who is good to you by your upholding the most just path and by the bounty toward the servants, ﴿their deeds﴾, leaving nothing of them, for nothing of them is hidden from Him. The context requires that "ma" in "lamma" in the lightened recitation be for emphasis, in the manner that has passed more than once: that when a negation is added within an affirmative context, it is as if it negates the opposite, as emphasis for the affirmed statement.

﴿Indeed, He is Aware of what they do﴾: he placed the adverbial phrase first for emphasizing the predicate ﴿Aware﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 112:

When you know that your condition with your nation is the condition of the Messengers with their peoples, that disagreement over the matter of the Messenger and the Book is inevitable, as God's established practice (sunnah ilahiyyah) has run, and that recompense for all deeds is inevitable, then ﴿So be upright﴾, meaning: bring the people to the utmost of your effort, because you are not charged except with yourself, and because He who sent you is not heedless of anything. Whoever is upright, uprightness is made to attend him.

Since it is certain that the one who commands the Prophet ﷺ is the one to whom all command belongs, he used the passive in his saying ﴿as you have been commanded﴾, meaning: just as your brothers among the prophets were upright in all the fundamentals and the subsidiaries, whether in yourself or in conveying to others, moderate between excess and deficiency, and that your breast should not be constricted by their mockery, their obstinacy, their demands for signs, and their desire that you leave out some of what is revealed to you of reproach against them and disparagement of their religion. Rather, declare the matter to them plainly, leave them and their desires. We manage the affair as We wish, according to what We know.

(p-391) Since the connecting element between the conjoined and the conjoined-to stands in place of emphasizing the concealed pronoun, He conjoined to it His saying ﴿and those who﴾, meaning: let those also who ﴿turn back﴾ from disbelief, believing ﴿with you﴾, be upright as they were commanded, leaving off anxiety over their slowness in victory, as al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i related from Khabbab ibn al-Arat, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was reclining on a cloak in the shade of the Ka'bah, and we had suffered severe hardship from the polytheists. We said: Will you not pray to Allah for us? He sat up, his face reddened, and said: 'Among those before you, a man would be dug a pit in the earth and placed in it, then a saw would be brought and placed upon his head, and he would be split in two, and that would not turn him from his religion. And he would be combed with iron combs, which would strip the flesh from his bones and sinews, and that would not turn him from his religion. By Allah, Allah will surely complete this matter, until a rider travels from San'a to Hadramawt fearing none but Allah and the wolf for his sheep, but you are hasty.'" And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "No verse was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ more severe or more difficult than this verse." And istiqamah is persistence in one direction.

Since it is a middle course between excess and deficiency, and since deficiency is hardly ever escaped except by the rare individual, and since it generally results in breaking the soul and belittling it and fear of Allah, while excess results in self-admiration, and perhaps leads a person to think that he is a lawgiver and thereby exits the religion, He passed over deficiency and forbade excess, saying ﴿and do not transgress﴾, meaning: do not exceed the limit in what you have been commanded or forbidden, by adding in excess. For Allah the Exalted commanded and forbade you only to refine your souls, not because He has need of that, and you will never be able to measure Allah with His due measure. The religion is firm; no one will strive against it except that it overcomes him. He, glorified be He, has been pleased from you with moderation in action together with good intentions. It is also possible that the meaning is: let blessing not make you exuberant, so that it takes you out of the path of uprightness to the right or to the left.

When He forbade excess, which is increase, explicitly, He thereby implied the prohibition of deficiency, which is falling short of what was commanded, allusively, *a fortiori*. He emphasized this by treating whoever is deficient or excessive as one who denies. So He said: ﴿Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do﴾ [Hud: 112]. He placed the adverbial phrase first because of what preceded it, the emphasis on seeing, ﴿Seeing﴾ [Hud: 112].

The root *ṭ-gh-y* (طغى) is both waw-based and ya-based in every arrangement, and it revolves around exceeding a limit together with height. Thus *al-ghiṭāʾ* (الغِطاء, "covering") is that by which a thing is concealed, raised above it. It does not conceal the whole of the thing unless it exceeds it, going beyond its limit. *Ghaṭṭā al-layl* (غطّى الليل) means the night covered, when it enveloped. Everything that rises high is *ghāṭin* (غاطٍ). *Ṭaghā al-sayl* (طغى السيل) means the torrent came with much water. *Ṭaghā al-baḥr* (طغى البحر) means its waves rose. *Al-ṭughyān* (الطُّغيان) is exceeding the limit in disobedience. *Al-ghāʾiṭ* and *al-ghayṭ* (الغائط والغيط) mean low-lying land, because such land, when its soil is good, is always moist, so what grows in it rises high and flourishes, exceeding the limit in that. From this comes *al-Ghūṭah* (الغوطة), the name of a place in Syria abundant in water and trees.

When He forbade excess in religion, He followed it with the prohibition of deficiency in it, through falling short in it by the lowering of aspirations [in a general way. Love for God and hatred for what opposes Him are the firmest handholds of faith, an allusion to its opposite, which is the firmest handhold of Satan]. So He said: ﴿And do not incline﴾, meaning, not even a little inclination. He said: ﴿toward those who wronged﴾, meaning, wrongdoing was found among them. He did not say "the wrongdoers," meaning by inclining toward them, such that your souls grow heavy toward them, to incline toward their deeds, even by consenting to them, imitating them, and adopting their appearance. The sum of the two verses is: do not wrong yourselves, and do not regard the deeds of the wrongdoers as good.

Al-Zamakhshari (الزمخشري) interpreted *rukūn* (الركون) as slight inclination. This is sound in meaning, but I have not seen it from other lexicographers. Al-Rummani (الرماني), who is closer to the truth, said: *al-rukūn* is settling upon a thing through love and pouring oneself toward it, and its opposite is aversion from it. On the second interpretation, *ṭaghaw* in ﴿you exceed﴾ [Hud: 112] is the specific following the general, and the verse alludes to His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you will leave aside some of what is revealed to you﴾ [Hud: 12].

﴿Then the Fire will touch you﴾, meaning, as a consequence of your inclining toward them, its touch will reach you, and you will not be able to escape from it by any kind of stratagem from yourselves. [And] among the honoring of the Prophet ﷺ is that He addressed him singly in commands to good deeds, while using the plural pronoun in prohibitions of evil deeds. Imam Abu Hayyan (الإمام أبو حيان) drew attention to this.

Since every existent other than God is under His subjugation and subject to His command, He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And you have not﴾. Since among the ranks and essences there is beyond His rank, Exalted is He, what no one but He, Glorified is He, can count, He introduced the preposition for partition and said: ﴿besides God﴾, meaning the Supreme King. He went to the utmost in negation and said: ﴿any protectors﴾, meaning, who might save you from His punishment. This is because *dūn* (دون) refers to what is lower, and it is closest to the direction of the bottom. The *walī* (الولي) is one specially entrusted with providing help when needed. He indicated that the victory of one who has no victor from God is impossible, by the particle of distance and the passive construction, and said: ﴿Then you will not be helped﴾, meaning, then if this and that have escaped you, how far you are from being given victory!

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 114:

Since it was already known from the ruling that preceded, namely that the human being is a place of incapacity and shortcoming, He followed that with the highest expiator of what incapacity necessitates and what slackness and weakness decree of minor sins, the most comprehensive of expiations, and the most conducive to uprightness. This indicates that the prayer, after faith, is the best of the acts of worship. So the Exalted said: ﴿And establish the prayer﴾ (p-395), meaning: perform it with evenness, ﴿at the two ends of the day﴾, that is, at dawn and at afternoon, as it was prescribed in Makkah at the beginning of the matter, before the Night Journey (al-Isra'). It is possible that the noon prayer (al-Zuhr) is also intended along with that, since it belongs to the second end. ﴿And at the approaches of the night﴾, meaning: groups, degrees and times; it is the plural of zulfah. ﴿Of the night﴾: it is possible that what is meant by it is the night prayer (tahajjud), for it was obligatory at the beginning of Islam; and it is possible that what is meant is the sunset prayer (maghrib) and the night prayer ('isha'), together with the witr, or the tahajjud. Then He gave the reason for that by His saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds﴾, meaning: all acts of obedience, the prayer and other than it, which are founded on the basis of faith, ﴿remove the evil deeds﴾, meaning: the minor sins. As for the major sins [which are expressed by al-fawahish (indecencies) and the like], it has already been mentioned in the story of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, at His saying: ﴿Then repent to Him﴾ [Hud: 90], that these are not expiated except by repentance, because of what it contains of an indication of disregard for the religion. Abstaining from them does not expiate them except when it is from a sound intention, as the form of the reflexive verb (ifti'al) in His saying: ﴿If you avoid﴾ [al-Nisa': 31] makes understood.

Al-Bukhari related in the Book of Tafsir, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that: "A man had touched a woman with a kiss, so he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and mentioned that to him, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ - the verse. The man said: 'Is this for me?' He said: 'It is for whoever acts upon it of my nation.'" This hadith supports the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that this verse is from this surah, which is Meccan and Medinan.

When this was completed in this excellent manner and this excellent order, the Exalted said (p-396), praising it so that its worth may be known and so that it may be adhered to: ﴿That﴾, meaning: the matter of lofty rank that has preceded, of encouragement and warning, consolation, and the teaching of the disease and its cure for deliverance from wretchedness, ﴿is a reminder﴾, meaning: a great reminder, ﴿for those who remember﴾, meaning: for those who have the capacity for remembrance and attention to it, with presence of heart, clarity of thought and penetrating understanding.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 115:

Since patience for the sake of God in the face of hardships is the highest of acts of obedience, He followed that with His saying: ﴿So be patient﴾, i.e., let there be from you patience in the acts of obedience and in refraining from sins, and do not abandon warning them of what you have been commanded, whatever it may be, and do not fear them, for the final outcome will be yours if you do so. Since the station of patience is difficult, and steadfastness in what is praiseworthy from it is especially perilous, and since the soul, because of its anxiety in many circumstances, is like one who rejects it, He emphasized His saying: ﴿Indeed﴾ patience is beneficence in its entirety, and indeed ﴿God﴾, i.e., the One encompassing the attributes of perfection, ﴿does not waste﴾, i.e., in any way whatsoever, ﴿the reward of the good-doers﴾, i.e., those who excel in the description of beneficence, to the extent that they worship God as though they see Him; therefore patience is easy for them. And that is because obedience is a burden, so it is not achieved except through patience, and everything other than it is the desire of the soul, in which there is no patience. Thus the entire religion is patience: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." Therefore the reward of the patient is magnified: ﴿Only those who are patient will be given their reward in full, without reckoning﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]. Praiseworthy patience is restraining the soul from going forth toward what is impermissible, such as abandoning the truth; its opposite is anxiety (jaza'). The poet said:

If you two are patient, patience is better in its outcome, and if you two are anxious, the matter is as you both see.

This is of the patience which is the well-known bitter thing, because it is the swallowing of the bitterness of the truth by restraining the soul from going forth toward what it desires, together with the restraint recognized by the Shari'ah and reason. Thus it is the most hateful thing to the soul. What helps one to it is sensing the honour and reward in adhering to the truth through obedience, knowing the good that follows in every respect, and the soul's habituation to it. Its application has come to be predominantly restricted to the truth, such that it is not permissible to apply it except to that. Said by al-Rummani.

[p. 398] When all that preceded pointed to the improbability that the obstinate would believe through any human contrivance, as the narratives almost express, and likewise the information that their worship is only out of imitation, and the divergence of Musa's people concerning his Book, which is guidance and mercy, and all of that serves to wean the listener from seeking what may pass through the mind, namely wishing that they would accede to what they propose or that he would refrain from some of the warning that vexes them, and since it is the nature of human beings to be slow to desist from such thoughts except after experience, this may have prompted someone to say: "If they were answered to their request, perhaps they would turn back from much of what they are engaged in." So this prompted them toward right guidance, and consequently it was said, as a rebuttal of this: ﴿Why then were there not﴾. It is also possible that its connection is this: when He mentioned the destruction of the earlier generations and the past nations, through what had passed, until He concluded with the command to be patient in doing good, in enjoining good and forbidding evil, it was possible that an objection would occur to the mind, saying: "What is the cause of that?" So He clarified that the cause of the destruction was turning away from forbidding the one who violates sacred limits, and the one who dares to tear down the noble veils and graze in the protected pasture, while they had the capacity, through what He, glory be to Him, had deposited in them of faculties and power to choose the side of good and turn away from the side of evil. So the Exalted said: ﴿Why then were there not﴾, with a form that admits of restriction, and in it is the sense of lamentation and regret, with regard to everyone who was in a similar state to theirs: ﴿of the generations﴾, i.e., the mighty ones who were destroyed, who existed in some period of time.

Since the intended meaning is the generations whose destruction was mentioned earlier, and their times were part of the bygone period, He used the preposition, saying: ﴿before you, there were people of﴾, i.e., possessors of ﴿remnant﴾, i.e., of preservation, goodness, and watchfulness over what would set them right. This is because the root *baqiya* revolves around the sense of remaining, and it entails strength, firmness, and preservation, from their saying: *ubqihi bi-quwwatika mālaka* (the form *ud'uhu*), i.e., preserve it with the preservation you give your property. It also entails watchfulness and observation: *baqītu al-shay'* means when you looked at it and kept watch over it. It also entails firmness: *baqiya baqā'an*, meaning it endured. And it entails goodness and excellence. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because a man keeps back the best and most excellent of what he brings out." And it is said: "So-and-so is of the remnant of a people," i.e., [p. 399] of their choice ones. The explanation of this will come in full at His saying, ﴿And We placed between them a barrier﴾ [al-Kahf: 52], God willing. ﴿who forbid﴾, i.e., they repeatedly renew the prohibition at all times, indicating the abundance of the corrupters ﴿from corruption﴾ [existing] ﴿in the land.﴾

Here, *lawlā* (a particle of reproach or lament) is like the one in Yunus, either reproachful or interrogative, as al-Rummani permitted both. It may also be restrictive (*takhsīṣiyyah*), as al-Zamakhshari said, and it is addressed to the listener, not to those destroyed. Since the verse includes the destruction of those who persisted in corruption, this constitutes the strongest exhortation to others to enjoin good and forbid evil, and the most complete threatening deterrent from committing the like of their condition, which would bring about [punishment] within the midst of their retribution. The placing of this verse after the verse on patience indicates that patience in enjoining good and forbidding evil is at its highest level. The verse also refers to His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾ [Hud: 12].

Since the three meanings all contain negation, the sense is: "There was none who would do that." Thus the exception in His saying, ﴿except a few﴾, is connected, i.e., righteous ones ﴿of those We rescued from among them.﴾ The apparent reading is that *min* is explanatory (*bayāniyyah*), meaning: they are the ones We rescued, for they forbade corruption. [He expressed it with rescue (*injā'*) because it indicates the goodness that motivates forbidding corruption, unlike *tanjiyah*, which indicates gradualness and thoroughness in rescue; had He used it, the meaning would be corrupted.] ﴿But those who did wrong followed﴾ the majority, i.e., those who committed wrong by abandoning the prohibition of corruption, and how fine is the unrestricted expression of it, without being qualified by "from among them." ﴿what﴾ [they were given]. Since what caused them to become insolent was prosperity itself, He used the passive in His saying, ﴿they were given luxury in it﴾, so the blessing made them insolent until they transgressed and became tyrants. ﴿And they were criminals﴾, i.e., characterized on the basis of firm habit by criminality, which is severing the cord of God permanently. So your Lord destroyed them for their criminality, and had it not been for that, He would not have done so, for their destruction, on the assumption that they were free from criminality, would be an injustice by their own accepted standards.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verse 117:

When it had become clear from what preceded that the lesson lies in the destruction and the deliverance being for the majority, he established, confirmed and clarified this with His saying: ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people are reformers.﴾ He, glory be to Him, was mentioned by the attribute that conveys beneficence, as affirmation and reassurance for him [the Prophet]. ﴿That He would destroy the towns﴾, meaning destruction in a general sense, ﴿unjustly﴾, meaning whatever injustice it was, small or great, ﴿while their people are reformers﴾, meaning in a state of injustice by bringing about their destruction while they are in the state of reform in which they are immersed. Thus the destruction would fall outside its proper place as people commonly understand it, while knowing that He has the right to do that in reality, since He is not questioned about what He does. Al-ihlak (destruction) is the bringing about of that which nullifies sensation; al-halak (perdition) is the loss of a thing, namely its being in such a state that it is not known where it is; and al-islah (reform) is the bringing about of that by which the affair becomes upright according to what reason calls for.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 118–119:**

(p-401) Since verses like these may give the impression that the faith of such people does not fall under the Will (al-mashi'ah), he removed that misconception by showing that the Will is separate from the command, saying: ﴿And if your Lord had willed﴾, that is, the One who is good to you in every goodness that increases you in rank, ﴿He would have made mankind﴾, that is, all of them, ﴿one community﴾ upon guidance. So He is able to make them all righteous and in agreement on faith, and He would not destroy them. But He did not will that. Rather, He willed their disagreement, and the matter follows His Will, so they disagreed. ﴿And they will not cease to be in disagreement﴾, that is, their disagreement remains constant, because they follow various religions, ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy﴾, that is, the One who is good to you by uniting them, by making them among the people of your obedience. For they do not disagree about the fundamentals of the truth. Since what has preceded may lead someone to ask: Why did He not turn their hearts toward guidance and turn them away from the causes of destruction, if He is able to? God, exalted is He, answered this, saying: ﴿And for that﴾, that is, for the disagreement, ﴿He created them﴾ [that is, He brought them into being and produced them from non-existence, and decreed them]. This is because, when He, glorified is He, fashioned them with dispositions of good and evil that necessitate disagreement due to their differences in these dispositions, they were made as if they had been created for it. They proceeded in accordance with destiny and decree, and it was not possible for them to proceed according to what reason calls for, namely that agreement is mercy and disagreement is vengeance. So a group of them deserved the Fire and a group deserved Paradise. This is not contrary to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56] (p-402) Rather, it is of the same kind. That is, when He, exalted is He, constituted them with weakness and granted them intellects together with setting up the proofs, this prepared them for worship, so they were as if they had been created for nothing but it. That is, "I did not create them except that they may know Me" through the enforcement of My decrees and My disposals concerning them, so that they worship, that is, submit to Me. Whoever among them is obedient is truly a worshipper, and whoever is disobedient is a worshipper in a figurative sense (majazan), that is, submissive to the command through its enforcement upon him and his inability to refrain, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15], and so on. It has thus become clear that creating them for worship alone contradicts creating them for disagreement, because their proceeding in His decree with disagreement is worship and prostration linguistically (lughatan). This is because the roots ʿ-b-d and s-j-d both revolve around submission, humility, and compliance, and by this everyone is a servant of Allah. Or the reference is to the locus of agreement and disagreement, so that His favor is manifest toward those He made firm, and His justice is manifest toward those He forsook.

Since this disagreement is the cause of disbelief, for which He sent His messengers to fight, it might be thought that it occurs without His Will. So he made clear that it is only by His desire, and there is no objection to Him, and he said: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾, that is, they hastened to what He created them for, turning away from His commands, and their intellects did not avail them. Then ﴿the word of your Lord﴾ was fulfilled, that is, the One who is good to you by subduing your enemies, which preceded in eternity, and it is: "By My might, I will surely fill Hell" (p-403) [that is] the one in which the tormented is met with scowling and frowning, ﴿with jinn﴾, that is, the kind of jinn [He mentioned them first because they are the origin of evil], then He generalized, saying: ﴿and mankind, all of them﴾. So they proceeded according to what He willed, and it was not possible for them, with their sound intellects and strong powers, to do other than surrender. Whoever says that He creates the actions of His servants, or that He has power over something, let him do otherwise, by reporting their agreement and then doing it so that his statement may be complete. Otherwise, let him know that he is a subordinate, subdued, and let him hear the messages of his Lord addressed to him with his body and his heart.

When Allah, glorified is He, had informed about what was done to the wrongdoing towns, and warned everyone who does their deeds of His might in this world and the Hereafter, and had commanded following His command and turning away from their disagreement, which He had decreed and willed, He connected to His saying, ﴿We relate to you﴾ [Hud: 100], His saying: ﴿And all [that] We relate﴾, meaning: and We relate ﴿to you﴾ every ﴿news﴾, that is, every very great report, ﴿of the accounts of the messengers﴾ with their peoples, the righteous among them and the corrupt, so it is general, to magnify the matter. The thing that drew these stories was what preceded in His saying: ﴿So perhaps you would leave some of what is revealed to you, and your breast would be constrained by it﴾ [Hud: 12], and so on. The seat of the breast is the heart, which is the fu'ad (the inner core of the heart), the organ by which the human being, and indeed the animal, subsists, and it is the hottest part of it. For this reason it is expressed by what is derived from fa'd, which is burning. Heat entails agitation and turning, from which the word "qalb" (heart) is derived, so the breast becomes constricted by it. He substituted for "kullan" (all) His saying: ﴿with which We firm up your fu'ad﴾, that is, a great firming, ﴿so that it settles in its place and is reassured, or its certainty increases, and the breast is not constricted by their saying: "Why has not a treasure been sent down to him, or an angel come with him?"﴾ [Hud: 12] and the like. By this it becomes clear that the general here is intended as specific, since the purpose for it is achieved, which is consolation, in view of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and your breast is constrained by it﴾ [Hud: 12], because sharing difficult matters makes what a person suffers from harm easier to bear, and informing about the punishments of the deniers in them is a comfort to the distressed. Tathbit (firming) is establishing a thing in place. Fu'ad is the organ whose nature is to be heated by the anger residing in it, from mufta'id, which is the hot place.

Since He had made clear that everything related to him of their reports entails this purpose, He made clear that it is not like the empty reports and the adorned, false narratives by which things are often justified, nor like what the historians transmit mixed with distortion. So He said: ﴿And there has come to you in this﴾, that is, in these reports, ﴿the truth﴾, that is, what is complete in its steadfastness, about which there is no doubt. The benefit of the adverbial phrase is emphasis, on account of the greatness of the purpose of His saying: ﴿So perhaps﴾ [Hud: 12] and its difficulty.

Since the truth is truth with respect to every person, He defined it, and He made indefinite what is specific to one people rather than another, so He said: ﴿and an admonition﴾, that is, something softening to the hearts, ﴿and a reminder﴾, that is, a very great remembrance, ﴿for the believers﴾, that is, those firmly rooted in faith. The verse has included taking lessons from the stories of the messengers, with what is in them of the excellence of their patience with their peoples and their striving in calling them to the worship of Allah in truth, and the reminder of good and evil and what each of them calls to of the consequences of benefit and harm, for steadfastness in all of that, following their example.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 11, verses 121–122:

When he mentioned the benefit of this truth, it was as if it were said: "Admonish them with it and remind them of it." So he joined to it his saying: ﴿And say﴾. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to his saying: ﴿and be patient﴾ [Hud: 115], meaning: be patient over what We have commanded you concerning conveying Our revelation and acting upon it, and say ﴿to those who﴾, meaning: this admonition has not affected them, so they ﴿do not believe﴾, meaning: faith will not be renewed for them, warning them: ﴿Act﴾, being firmly established ﴿in your position﴾, meaning: your way, by which you are able to act.

Since acting was obligatory upon him ﷺ and upon everyone who followed him, they are certainly acting, whether the disbelievers act or not. He said, emphasizing it in order to deny the disbelievers' hope that they would persist in their action contrary to theirs, despite the harm that reaches them because of it, and leaving it free of the "fa" of causation [for that and the resumption]: ﴿Indeed, we﴾ [meaning: I and those with me] ﴿are acting﴾ [meaning: our action is established, we do not turn away from it; for what belongs to God is lasting through His permanence, glory be to Him]. He omitted the second nun (p-406) relying on the general emphasis, since it is sufficient in informing of resolute intention. In this there is a courtesy, by way of indicating that the future is a matter that no one but God has knowledge of, so one should not exaggerate the emphasis concerning it to anyone other than Him. This is unlike what is in Surah Fussilat, which is spoken on the tongues of the disbelievers.

﴿And wait﴾, meaning: wait for what you are awaiting of Our subjugation. ﴿Indeed, we are waiting﴾, meaning: for what God has promised us concerning your affair, for God will destroy them and save you, because He has knowledge of the unseen state of you and them, and is capable over you.

Al-intizar (waiting) is seeking to attain what comes of a matter that can be looked toward. Al-tawaqqu' (expectation) is seeking what is estimated to occur. Both occur in good and evil, and with knowledge and with doubt. Al-tarajji (hoping) occurs only with good and with doubt.

When this threat encompassed knowledge and power, He said, connecting it by a conjunction to what its implied meaning is: "To Allah belongs all that is witnessed of our affair, your affair, and the affair of the Knower of the Unseen and the Witnessed, all of it, whatever has been from the beginning of our affairs." ﴿To Allah﴾, i.e., the One alone who encompasses everything, along with that, ﴿belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, i.e., all that its knowledge has been hidden from the servants, so He has perfect knowledge. [Among it is what He forbids, even if the ignorant think it is outside His power, because of the prohibition made manifest against it and His disliking of it.]

Since the context here is that He, glorified is He, created the creation, their essences and their meanings, for differing, and since His threatening them over sins may give the impression that it is without His will, a Jahil might say: "I am very far removed from those who oppose His allies," and it is the habit of creatures that whoever opposes them is outside their command. The answer, on the assumption of accepting this apparent matter, was: ﴿So to Him belongs the whole affair, apparent and hidden.﴾ [﴿And to Him﴾, i.e., alone, ﴿all matters are returned﴾ [after it had appeared to the ignorant that they had gone out from Him]. Return (rujū') is the going of a thing back to where it began.] ﴿The whole affair﴾ is in the present state under obscurity and concealment, and in the end it is under manifestness, clarity and disclosure. So He encompasses power just as He encompasses knowledge, and so your affair and the affair of your enemies must return to Him, i.e., He acts in it as one to whom the affair returns, so He rewards the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. For this reason, from the attribution of all matters [to Him] He drew the consequence: ﴿So worship Him﴾, i.e., alone, with worship in which there is no admixture, ﴿and rely upon Him﴾, depending upon Him in all your affairs, ﴿for He is the Strong, the Firm﴾. In placing the command of worship before reliance, there is an alert that it is only worship that benefits the worshipper.

Since it is the habit that the knower may be heedless, He, glorified is He, declared Himself free of that, and said, encouraging and warning: ﴿And your Lord is not heedless of what you do﴾, i.e., the One who benefits you by what He does, by the all-encompassing nature of His action, as a benefit. He went to the extreme in negation, saying: ﴿not heedless of what you do﴾ [and there is no threat more emphatic than knowledge]. This is exactly the import of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A Book whose verses have been perfected, then detailed, from One Wise, Aware﴾ [Hud: 1], ﴿that you worship none but Allah; indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ [Hud: 2].
